input:
[Transcript - practice manager call, Tues 14:10]

CONSULTANT: Talk me through what happens when a patient has private treatment.
DEBORAH (practice manager): So the dentist writes the treatment on the paper chart while the patient's in the chair. Codes, materials, whether it was a composite or an onlay, all of it goes on the chart.
CONSULTANT: And then?
DEBORAH: The charts come to the front desk in a tray at the end of the session. I sit down about half five, six o'clock and type them into SOE - that's our practice management system - and raise the invoice.
CONSULTANT: Same day?
DEBORAH: Supposed to be. If we've had a busy list it slips to the next morning, sometimes Friday if it's been a bad week.
CONSULTANT: What triggers it, the chart arriving?
DEBORAH: Yes, the tray. If a chart doesn't make it into the tray I don't know it exists.
CONSULTANT: Does that happen?
DEBORAH: More than I'd like. Mr Achebe does a lot of implant work and he'll take a chart into his office to write up his notes and I'll find it a fortnight later. That treatment's just not been billed.
CONSULTANT: Who chases payment?
DEBORAH: Me. I run an aged debt report out of SOE on the last Friday of the month and phone anyone over 30 days.
CONSULTANT: Card payments at the desk?
DEBORAH: Most people pay on the day at reception, we've got a Worldpay terminal. It's the plans and the bigger treatments that get invoiced.
CONSULTANT: And the write-up handwriting?
DEBORAH: Honestly some of it I have to go and ask about. That's another delay.

gold.objective: Turn private dental treatment recorded on paper charts into invoices raised in the practice management system, and recover payment on the resulting debt.
gold.trigger: A completed paper treatment chart arrives in the tray at the front desk at the end of a clinical session.
inputs_data_required: Handwritten paper treatment chart (codes, materials, whether composite or onlay)
Aged debt report from SOE
Patient contact details for payment chasing
current_process: Dentist writes treatment, codes and materials onto the paper chart while the patient is in the chair
Charts are placed in a tray at the front desk at the end of the session
Deborah types the charts into SOE at around 17:30-18:00 and raises the invoice
Where the list has been busy, typing slips to the next morning or to Friday
Most patients pay at reception on the day by Worldpay terminal; plans and larger treatments are invoiced
Deborah runs an aged debt report from SOE on the last Friday of the month and phones anyone over 30 days
bottlenecks_and_risks: Charts that never reach the tray are invisible to billing - Mr Achebe takes implant charts to his office and they surface a fortnight later, by which time the treatment is unbilled
The tray is the only trigger, so there is no check that every treated patient has been billed
Illegible handwriting forces Deborah to go back and ask the clinician, adding further delay
Billing depends entirely on one person; a busy list pushes invoicing into the following week
Debt chasing happens only once a month, so a slipped invoice plus monthly chasing can leave treatment unpaid for 60+ days
recommended_improved_process: Dentist records treatment directly into SOE chairside, or dictates it, so the clinical record is the billing record
SOE automatically raises a draft invoice for every completed private treatment item at the end of each session
A daily exception report lists patients seen with no invoice raised, sent to Deborah each morning
Deborah reviews and releases the day's draft invoices rather than keying them
Invoices are issued the same day with a payment link; card payments at the desk continue to settle in SOE
Automated payment reminders are sent at 7, 14 and 28 days before any human chase
Deborah works a weekly exceptions-and-escalations list instead of a monthly aged debt sweep
ai_agent_steps: An AI agent can generate the daily 'seen but not invoiced' exception report by reconciling the SOE appointment list against raised invoices
An AI agent can draft the invoice narrative from the structured treatment items before Deborah reviews and releases it
An AI agent can send and escalate the automated payment reminders at 7, 14 and 28 days and flag non-responders
An AI agent can summarise the weekly exceptions-and-escalations list, ranking debts by age and value
human_approvals_controls: Deborah reviews and releases every draft invoice before it is issued
The treating clinician confirms the treatment items recorded in SOE at the end of the session
Write-offs and disputed charges require the practice manager's approval, outside the automated reminder cycle
A human makes contact before any account is referred to formal recovery

input:
[Recorded call - owner, 90-cover gastropub with a function room]

INTERVIEWER: You do private hire - weddings, wakes, birthdays. How does the money side work?
TOM: It all starts with an enquiry, usually a message on Facebook or someone rings up. I take it from there myself, nobody else does functions.
INTERVIEWER: Then what?
TOM: I get their number and we move onto WhatsApp. That's where everything happens. Menu choices, numbers, dietaries, whether they want the room dressed, what time the bar closes. All of it, in the thread.
INTERVIEWER: Deposit?
TOM: £200 to hold the date, bank transfer. I check my banking app and if it's landed I put the date in the wall diary in the office.
INTERVIEWER: And the final invoice?
TOM: After the event. I scroll back up the WhatsApp thread, work out what we agreed, add the bar tab off the till report, and type an invoice in Sage. Then I email it.
INTERVIEWER: How long does the scrolling take?
TOM: A wedding thread might be four months of messages. An hour, easy. And I've got maybe six or seven going at once so threads blur.
INTERVIEWER: Do things get missed?
TOM: Definitely. Corkage is the big one. We agree a corkage rate in message 40 and I forget by the time I invoice. Extra canapés too.
INTERVIEWER: Does anyone check the invoice before it goes?
TOM: No. It's just me.
INTERVIEWER: Payment terms?
TOM: I say seven days. Some pay, some don't, and then I'm chasing on WhatsApp again.

gold.objective: Invoice private-hire functions (weddings, wakes, birthdays) at a gastropub and collect payment after the event.
gold.trigger: A private hire event has taken place and the final invoice needs to be raised.

participants: Bar/till staff whose report supplies the bar tab

inputs_data_required: The WhatsApp thread with the client (menu choices, numbers, dietaries, room dressing, bar closing time, corkage rate)
Till report for the bar tab
£200 deposit confirmation from the banking app
The wall diary date entry
current_process: Enquiry arrives by Facebook message or phone and Tom handles it himself
Conversation moves to WhatsApp, where menu, numbers, dietaries, room dressing and bar times are all agreed
A £200 deposit is taken by bank transfer; Tom checks the banking app and writes the date in the office wall diary
After the event Tom scrolls back through the WhatsApp thread to reconstruct what was agreed
He adds the bar tab from the till report and types an invoice in Sage
The invoice is emailed on stated seven day terms; unpaid ones are chased back on WhatsApp
bottlenecks_and_risks: Reconstructing a four-month WhatsApp thread takes about an hour per wedding, and with six or seven threads running at once they blur together
Items agreed mid-thread are forgotten at invoicing - corkage is the recurring loss, plus extra canapés
Nobody checks the invoice before it goes out because Tom is the only person involved, so errors reach the client
Only the £200 deposit is secured; the entire balance is at risk until after the event
Seven day terms are stated but not enforced, and chasing happens on the same informal channel as the booking
recommended_improved_process: Capture the agreed package on a structured function sheet at booking, not in free chat
Record every variation (menu, numbers, corkage, extras) against the function sheet as it is agreed
Take a staged deposit and interim payment schedule rather than £200 alone
Generate the invoice from the function sheet plus the till bar tab, not from the message history
Have a second person check the invoice against the function sheet before sending
Issue invoices with a payment link and automated reminders on the stated terms
ai_agent_steps: An AI agent can extract agreed items and changes from the WhatsApp thread and propose updates to the function sheet
An AI agent can flag chargeable items agreed in conversation but missing from the draft invoice, such as corkage
An AI agent can issue the automated payment reminders on the stated seven day terms
An AI agent can reconcile the till bar tab to the function before the invoice is drafted
human_approvals_controls: Tom approves the function sheet and every variation before it becomes chargeable
A second person checks the invoice against the function sheet before it is sent
Discounts or waived charges require the owner's explicit approval
Escalation of a non-paying client to formal recovery is a human decision

input:
Workshop notes - digital agency, finance & ops session
Present: managing partner (Elin), finance assistant (Kofi), two account directors

Process in scope: monthly retainer billing.

- 19 retainer clients. Retainers are fixed monthly fees, but every contract includes an hours allowance with overage billed at £95/hr.
- Billing is meant to go out on the 1st working day of the month. It has not gone out on time in the last nine months.
- Blocker: overage can't be calculated until timesheets are complete in Harvest. Staff are asked to fill Harvest daily. Actual behaviour: most people fill it in on the 4th or 5th for the whole previous month, from memory and their calendar.
- Kofi chases by Slack DM. He described sending "the same eleven messages every month".
- Once Harvest is complete, Kofi exports a time report per client, compares hours used against the contracted allowance (held in a separate Google Sheet, one tab per client), and works out overage.
- Overage over £500 is supposed to be flagged to the account director to warn the client before it's invoiced. Elin said this "sometimes" happens.
- Kofi raises invoices in Xero manually, one at a time, copying the retainer line and adding an overage line.
- Elin reviews the batch before sending. This review is usually a quick look at totals.
- Invoices go out around the 8th-10th. Terms are 14 days, so cash lands later than the model assumes.
- Two clients have disputed overage in the last year because the reconstructed timesheets showed work they said they hadn't authorised.
- Recovery rate on overage is not measured.

gold.objective: Bill 19 retainer clients monthly, including hours used above the contracted allowance.
gold.trigger: The start of a new month, when billing is due to go out on the first working day.

owner_and_participants.owner: Kofi, the finance assistant (Elin, the managing partner, reviews)

inputs_data_required: Completed Harvest timesheets for the previous month
Contracted hours allowance per client (held in a separate Google Sheet, one tab per client)
Overage rate of £95/hr
Retainer fee per client
current_process: Billing is due on the first working day of the month
Staff are asked to complete Harvest daily but most fill it in on the 4th or 5th for the whole previous month from memory and their calendar
Kofi chases by Slack DM, sending the same eleven messages every month
Kofi exports a time report per client and compares hours used against the contracted allowance held in a separate Google Sheet
Overage over £500 is supposed to be flagged to the account director to warn the client, which happens only sometimes
Kofi raises invoices in Xero manually, copying the retainer line and adding an overage line
Elin reviews the batch with a quick look at totals, and invoices go out around the 8th-10th on 14 day terms
bottlenecks_and_risks: Billing cannot start until timesheets are complete, so invoices have not gone out on time in nine months and land around the 8th-10th
Timesheets reconstructed from memory days later are unreliable, and two clients have disputed overage on the basis that the reconstructed time showed unauthorised work
The £500 overage warning to clients happens only sometimes, so clients are surprised by charges they could have been told about
Contract allowances live in a separate spreadsheet from the time data, so every client requires a manual lookup and comparison
Invoices are raised one at a time by hand in Xero, and the review is a glance at totals rather than a check
14 day terms applied to invoices issued a week late means cash lands materially later than the business model assumes
Overage recovery rate is not measured, so nobody knows how much billable work is lost
recommended_improved_process: Enforce daily time entry with an automated lock or reminder before the month closes
Hold contracted hours allowances in Harvest against each client rather than a separate sheet
Generate the overage calculation automatically from Harvest at month end
Notify the account director and the client automatically once overage passes £500, before invoicing
Produce the invoice batch in Xero from the Harvest data rather than keying line by line
Have Elin review an exceptions list - disputed, unusual or large overage - rather than all totals
Report monthly on billing date achieved, overage billed and overage recovery rate
ai_agent_steps: An AI agent can chase incomplete timesheets daily and escalate individuals before the month-end cut-off
An AI agent can calculate overage against each client's allowance and draft the client warning once it passes £500
An AI agent can build the draft invoice batch in Xero from Harvest data
An AI agent can produce the monthly reporting on billing date, overage billed and recovery rate
human_approvals_controls: The account director approves and sends the overage warning to the client before invoicing
Elin reviews and releases the invoice batch, focusing on the exceptions list
Any overage write-off or discount requires the managing partner's approval
Disputed overage is investigated and resolved by a person, not adjusted automatically

input:
Quick notes - gym, first call (20 mins, cut short)

- Membership is monthly direct debit. Talked about what happens when one bounces.
- A report comes through once a month listing the failed ones. It's a PDF. Wasn't clear who sends it or what it comes out of - "it just arrives".
- Someone on the duty manager rota works through it and rings the members. Not the same person each month. Couldn't get a name for who owns this.
- If they get hold of the member they ask them to pay on the card machine next time they're in, or take it over the phone.
- If they can't get hold of them, nothing much happens. The member keeps swiping in.
- Asked how many failures a month - "a fair few", no number. Asked what the value is - didn't know.
- Asked at what point access is suspended. Answer was that it's meant to happen but nobody could say after how long or who does it.
- Some members apparently owe several months.
- Asked whether the failures are ever re-presented automatically. Nobody was sure.
- Didn't establish what the process is for members who cancel their DD at the bank without telling the gym.
- Ran out of time. Need a second call with whoever actually runs the report.

gold.objective: Recover membership payments where a monthly direct debit has failed.
gold.trigger: A monthly report listing failed direct debits arrives; the input does not establish who sends it or what produces it.

participants: Whoever is on the duty manager rota that month (not the same person each month)
Members whose direct debit has failed

inputs_data_required: The monthly PDF report of failed direct debits
Member contact details for calling
current_process: A report listing the failed direct debits arrives once a month as a PDF; the input does not establish its source
Someone on the duty manager rota works through it and rings the members; it is not the same person each month
Where the member is reached, they are asked to pay on the card machine next time they are in, or payment is taken over the phone
Where the member cannot be reached, nothing further happens and the member continues to swipe in
bottlenecks_and_risks: Nobody owns the process - it rotates among duty managers with no named accountable person, so failures fall between people
Members who cannot be reached keep using the club while owing money, and some apparently owe several months
There is no defined point at which access is suspended, and nobody could say after how long or who would do it
The volume and value of failed payments is unknown ('a fair few'), so the revenue leak cannot be sized or prioritised
It could not be established whether failures are automatically re-presented, so collections may be being abandoned unnecessarily
There is no process at all for members who cancel their direct debit at the bank without telling the club
The report arrives only monthly, so a failure can be up to a month old before anyone acts
recommended_improved_process: Name a single accountable owner for failed payment recovery
Receive failure notifications from the payment provider as they occur rather than in a monthly batch
Automatically re-present failed collections once before any human contact
Contact the member by automated message immediately after a failed re-presentation, with a payment link
Define and apply an access suspension rule at a stated number of days or failed payments
Detect bank-side cancellations from the provider feed and treat them as a cancellation event
Report monthly on failure volume, value, recovery rate and debt outstanding
ai_agent_steps: An AI agent can process the payment provider's failure notifications daily and trigger re-presentation and member contact
An AI agent can send the automated payment request messages with a payment link and escalate non-responders
An AI agent can identify bank-side direct debit cancellations from the provider feed and raise them as cancellation events
An AI agent can produce the monthly failure volume, value and recovery rate report
human_approvals_controls: The named owner approves suspension of a member's access before it takes effect
A person handles any member who disputes the charge or raises hardship
Write-off of an unrecoverable balance requires management approval
A person confirms a bank-side cancellation as a genuine membership cancellation before the record is closed

input:
WHOLESALE ORDER TO CASH
Documented process, v2, held by the operations coordinator

1. Purpose
To describe how orders from trade stockists are converted into invoices and payments. Direct-to-consumer orders are out of scope; those are paid at checkout.

2. Trigger
A stockist places an order. Orders arrive by three routes: the wholesale portal on the Shopify store (draft order), by email to the trade address, or verbally to the founder at a trade show.

3. Steps
3.1 The operations coordinator (Beth) creates or confirms the order in Shopify as a draft order at the stockist's price tier.
3.2 The draft order is sent to the 3PL by email as a CSV export for picking.
3.3 The 3PL confirms despatch and returns tracking, usually within two working days.
3.4 Beth exports the day's despatched wholesale orders from Shopify to CSV.
3.5 Beth opens Xero and creates a sales invoice for each despatched order, re-keying the customer, the lines and the values from the CSV. There is no integration between Shopify and Xero for wholesale orders.
3.6 The invoice is emailed from Xero on 30 day terms.
3.7 Payments are matched in Xero against the bank feed.
3.8 Overdue invoices are identified by Beth from the Xero aged receivables report and chased by email.

4. Known issues recorded at last review
Re-keying takes approximately half a day per week and errors have reached customers, including one invoice raised at retail rather than wholesale prices. Trade show orders are frequently not entered until after the goods have shipped. Where a stockist part-pays, the balance is not separately tracked. Nobody chases beyond two emails; there is no escalation step or stop-supply rule.

gold.objective: Convert trade stockist orders into invoices and collect payment, from order receipt through despatch to cash.
gold.trigger: A stockist places an order - via the wholesale portal on the Shopify store as a draft order, by email to the trade address, or verbally to the founder at a trade show.
inputs_data_required: The stockist's order and price tier
CSV export of the day's despatched wholesale orders from Shopify
Despatch confirmation and tracking from the 3PL
Xero aged receivables report
systems_involved: Shopify (wholesale portal, draft orders, price tiers)
Xero (sales invoices, bank feed, aged receivables)
current_process: Beth creates or confirms the order in Shopify as a draft order at the stockist's price tier
The draft order is exported as CSV and emailed to the 3PL for picking
The 3PL confirms despatch and returns tracking, usually within two working days
Beth exports the day's despatched wholesale orders from Shopify to CSV
Beth creates a sales invoice in Xero for each despatched order, re-keying customer, lines and values - there is no integration for wholesale orders
The invoice is emailed from Xero on 30 day terms and payments are matched against the bank feed
Beth identifies overdue invoices from the Xero aged receivables report and chases by email
bottlenecks_and_risks: Re-keying Shopify exports into Xero takes about half a day a week and has produced errors that reached customers, including an invoice raised at retail rather than wholesale prices
Trade show orders are frequently not entered until after the goods have shipped, so stock and invoicing lag the physical movement
Where a stockist part-pays, the balance is not separately tracked, so partial debts are invisible
Chasing stops after two emails with no escalation step and no stop-supply rule, so bad debt is allowed to accumulate while supply continues
The whole order-to-cash chain depends on Beth manually bridging Shopify and Xero, with no cover
Despatch to the 3PL is by emailed CSV, so a missed or mis-sent file stops picking with no systemic alert
recommended_improved_process: Integrate Shopify wholesale orders to Xero so invoices are raised automatically on despatch
Connect the 3PL by API or portal rather than emailed CSV, with despatch confirmations flowing back automatically
Enter trade show orders into Shopify at the show on a tablet, before shipping
Track part-payments against the invoice so outstanding balances are visible
Define an escalation ladder for overdue invoices ending in a stop-supply rule at a stated age or value
Report weekly on debtor days, part-paid invoices and accounts approaching the stop-supply threshold
ai_agent_steps: An AI agent can raise the Xero invoice automatically from the Shopify despatch record, removing the re-keying step
An AI agent can run the escalation ladder for overdue invoices and flag accounts hitting the stop-supply threshold
An AI agent can reconcile part-payments to invoices and surface outstanding balances
An AI agent can produce the weekly debtor days and stop-supply report
human_approvals_controls: Beth reviews the automatically raised invoices before they are issued, at least during a parallel-run period
The founder approves any decision to stop supply to a stockist
Price tier changes and manual price overrides require approval before invoicing
A person handles any stockist disputing an invoice

input:
JOB COMPLETION TO INVOICE
Written procedure, domestic and commercial plumbing contractor (5 engineers)

Purpose: to record how completed work is turned into a customer invoice.

Trigger: an engineer completes a job on site.

Steps:
1. The engineer completes a duplicate paper job sheet in the van, recording the customer, address, work done, parts used and hours on site. The customer signs where they are present.
2. The engineer photographs the job sheet on his phone and sends the photograph to the office WhatsApp group. The paper copy remains in the van.
3. The office administrator saves the photographs to a folder and works through them, normally on Wednesdays and Fridays.
4. Parts used are priced from the merchant's trade list. Where a part is not on the list the administrator asks the engineer.
5. An invoice is raised in QuickBooks and emailed to the customer on 14 day terms. Domestic customers are asked to pay on the day where possible.
6. Paper job sheets are collected from the vans when the engineer next visits the office and are filed by month.

Recorded issues:
- Photographs are frequently blurred, cut off at the edge, or taken in poor light. The administrator estimates ten to fifteen per week require a follow-up call to the engineer.
- Some job sheets are never photographed. These are found in the van weeks later, by which time the customer disputes the detail.
- Handwriting on the hours column is often ambiguous.
- The gap between completion and invoice averages nine days and has been as long as six weeks.
- No check is made that every job booked in the diary has resulted in an invoice.
- Parts fitted but not written on the sheet are not billed.

gold.objective: Turn completed plumbing jobs into customer invoices, from the on-site job sheet to an emailed invoice.
gold.trigger: An engineer completes a job on site.

participants: Customers, who sign the job sheet where present

inputs_data_required: Duplicate paper job sheet recording customer, address, work done, parts used and hours on site
Photograph of the job sheet sent to the office WhatsApp group
The merchant's trade price list for pricing parts
systems_involved: WhatsApp (office group receiving job sheet photographs)
current_process: The engineer completes a duplicate paper job sheet in the van recording customer, address, work done, parts used and hours; the customer signs where present
The engineer photographs the job sheet and sends it to the office WhatsApp group; the paper copy stays in the van
The administrator saves the photographs and works through them, normally on Wednesdays and Fridays
Parts are priced from the merchant's trade list; where a part is not listed the administrator asks the engineer
An invoice is raised in QuickBooks and emailed on 14 day terms, with domestic customers asked to pay on the day where possible
Paper job sheets are collected from vans when the engineer next visits the office and filed by month
bottlenecks_and_risks: Ten to fifteen photographs a week are blurred, cut off or badly lit and require a follow-up call to the engineer, adding rework to every billing run
Some job sheets are never photographed and are found in the van weeks later, by which time the customer disputes the detail
Ambiguous handwriting in the hours column means billable time is guessed or queried
The gap between completion and invoice averages nine days and has reached six weeks, directly delaying cash
No check is made that every job in the diary resulted in an invoice, so jobs can be completed and never billed
Parts fitted but not written on the sheet are not billed at all
Batching invoicing to Wednesdays and Fridays adds delay on top of the collection lag
recommended_improved_process: Replace the paper job sheet with a mobile job app capturing customer, work done, parts and hours as structured data with a customer signature on screen
Capture parts against the job from a priced catalogue at the point of use, rather than writing them by hand
Raise the invoice automatically from the completed job record on the day of completion
Run a daily exception report of diary jobs completed with no invoice raised
Issue invoices with a payment link and automated reminders on the 14 day terms
Report weekly on completion-to-invoice days and on jobs missing parts or hours
ai_agent_steps: An AI agent can produce the daily exception report of completed jobs with no invoice raised
An AI agent can validate the job record for missing hours or parts before the invoice is generated and prompt the engineer
An AI agent can transcribe legacy photographed job sheets into the structured format during transition, flagging illegible fields
An AI agent can send the automated payment reminders on the 14 day terms
human_approvals_controls: The administrator reviews and releases invoices before they are sent, at least during transition
The engineer confirms the job record, including hours and parts, before it is submitted
Any invoice raised from an incomplete or illegible record requires the administrator to confirm the detail with the engineer
Write-offs or price adjustments require the owner's approval

input:
Subject: our billing, since you asked

Hi Tom,

You asked me to describe how we bill the fixed fee clients. I've written it as it happens rather than as it's supposed to happen.

We've got about 380 clients on a fixed monthly fee, direct debit through GoCardless. That bit's fine, it just goes.

The problem is everything outside the fixed fee. Extra work. A client rings up about a mortgage reference, or wants us to deal with an HMRC letter, or asks us to do a company formation, or their bookkeeping is a disaster and we spend two days fixing it. That's all chargeable in theory.

Now, our engagement letters say clearly that additional work is billed at our standard hourly rates and that a quote will be given in advance. That's the policy, it's been the policy since 2018.

In practice, at the end of the quarter I sit down with the client list and think about who I've done stuff for. I bill from memory. I'll put £400 on one, £250 on another. I don't have a record of the time because our people only put time on jobs, not on ad hoc bits, and half the ad hoc bits are done by me on a phone call.

I should say - Kevin, my fellow partner, is adamant that nothing goes out without a quote first and that he always quotes in advance and always has. He genuinely believes that's the firm's process. He also bills quarterly from memory exactly like I do, I've watched him do it. So I don't know how both of those can be true, but that's what he'd tell you if you asked him.

Anyway. Some clients get billed for things others get for free. Some argue and I write it off, which I also don't record. I'd guess we're missing £60-80k a year but that's a finger in the air.

We use Xero for our own books, IRIS for compliance jobs, and time is recorded in IRIS but nobody does it properly.

Angela

gold.objective: Bill approximately 380 fixed-fee clients and, separately, recover additional work done outside the fixed fee.
gold.trigger: The end of a quarter, when the writer sits down with the client list and bills additional work from memory; the fixed fee itself is collected automatically by direct debit.

owner_and_participants.owner: Angela (the writer, partner); Kevin, a fellow partner, bills his own clients the same way
participants: Staff who record time on jobs in IRIS

inputs_data_required: The client list
The partner's recollection of ad hoc work done
Engagement letters stating additional work is billed at standard hourly rates with a quote given in advance
Time recorded in IRIS on jobs (not on ad hoc work)
current_process: About 380 clients pay a fixed monthly fee by direct debit through GoCardless, which runs without intervention
Additional work arises - mortgage references, HMRC letters, company formations, fixing a client's bookkeeping
Engagement letters state that additional work is billed at standard hourly rates and that a quote will be given in advance
At the end of the quarter Angela goes through the client list and bills from memory, putting £400 on one client and £250 on another
No time record supports these bills - staff record time on jobs but not on ad hoc work, and much of it is done by a partner on a phone call
Where a client argues, the amount is written off, and the write-off is not recorded
bottlenecks_and_risks: The stated process and the actual process contradict each other, and the contradiction is held within the firm itself - Kevin is adamant that nothing goes out without a quote first and believes that is the firm's process, while also billing quarterly from memory exactly as Angela does, which she has watched him do
Billing from memory at quarter end means work done in month one is invoiced up to three months later, or forgotten entirely
The engagement letter promise of an advance quote is not kept, so clients are surprised by charges they never agreed
Some clients are billed for work others receive free, with no basis for the difference
Write-offs following client argument are not recorded, so the leakage is invisible
Estimated £60-80k a year is being missed, and that figure is explicitly a finger in the air because no data exists
recommended_improved_process: Require ad hoc work to be recorded against the client at the point it is done, including partner phone calls
Issue a written quote or scope confirmation before additional work starts, as the engagement letter promises
Bill additional work monthly from the recorded time rather than quarterly from memory
Record every write-off with a reason and an approver
Reconcile the firm's stated process with actual practice and re-brief both partners
Report quarterly on additional work billed, written off and recovery rate by partner
ai_agent_steps: An AI agent can capture ad hoc work from partners' calendars, call logs and emails and prompt them to confirm a chargeable entry
An AI agent can draft the advance quote for additional work from the recorded scope
An AI agent can produce the monthly additional-work billing schedule from recorded time for partner review
An AI agent can report on write-offs and recovery rate by partner
human_approvals_controls: A partner confirms each captured ad hoc entry as chargeable before it enters the billing schedule
The client's acceptance of the advance quote is obtained before additional work starts
Write-offs require a recorded reason and an approver other than the partner who raised the bill
Partners review and release the monthly additional-work billing schedule

input:
Subject: the chair rent thing

Hey Lucy,

So you asked about how I bill the girls who rent chairs. It's four of them now plus me, and it's turning into a proper headache.

The deal is they pay a weekly rent for the chair. Three are on £180 a week flat. Nadia is on £120 plus 10% of anything over £900 in takings, because she was building her column up when she started and I said I'd do her a deal. That was two years ago and she's now my busiest, so that percentage matters.

What I do on a Sunday night is I go into Fresha, look at each of their columns for the week, add up what they took, work out what they owe, and write it on a bit of paper. Then I leave the notes on the shelf in the staff room on Monday and they pay me - two by bank transfer, one by cash, one keeps saying she'll set up a standing order.

Fresha does the takings but they all handle their own payments, so some of their clients pay them directly on their own card readers and that never touches Fresha. So Nadia's percentage is based on what I can see, which isn't everything, and we both know that.

They also use my colour stock. They're supposed to buy their own but they don't, they just grab a tube, and then I try and remember to add it to their note. I mostly forget.

Two of them owe me from before Christmas. There's no record of what's outstanding except the notes I write, and I don't keep copies.

None of it goes near the accounts properly. My accountant just gets a figure for chair rent income at year end that I work out from my bank statements, and it never matches what I think it should be.

I don't think any of them are trying it on. It's just a mess.

Priya x

CONSULTANT: You're doing the landlord statements now. Show me.
NAOMI: Right. So this is the client account transactions report out of Reapit. Everything that's gone in and out for the month.
CONSULTANT: And it exports to?
NAOMI: Excel. But it comes out one line per transaction, all landlords mixed together.
CONSULTANT: So then?
NAOMI: I sort it by landlord and I copy each landlord's block into their statement.
CONSULTANT: Each landlord has their own file?
NAOMI: Each landlord has a tab in this workbook. There's 212 tabs.
CONSULTANT: Ok.
NAOMI: Then I've got a second spreadsheet with the fee structure - what percentage we take, whether they're on full management or let-only, whether they've got a fixed fee for the safety certs. That's not in Reapit properly so it lives here.
CONSULTANT: You look up each landlord in that?
NAOMI: Yes. And a third one for the contractor invoices, because the contractor invoices get paid out of client account but they come to us as PDFs and I have to key them in to allocate them to the right property.
CONSULTANT: Three spreadsheets and the system.
NAOMI: Four if you count the one for the ones on a payment holiday.
CONSULTANT: How long does month end take?
NAOMI: Four days. Sometimes five. I do nothing else that week.
CONSULTANT: Then what happens?
NAOMI: I print each tab to PDF and email them out one at a time. 212 emails.
CONSULTANT: Manually?
NAOMI: Yes.
CONSULTANT: Does anyone check them?
NAOMI: My manager spot-checks a few. Not all.
CONSULTANT: Errors?
NAOMI: Every month there's a few. Landlords email back. Usually a contractor invoice on the wrong property, or a fee percentage that's changed and I've used the old one.
CONSULTANT: What if you're off?

[Interview - sales ledger clerk and transport supervisor]

INTERVIEWER: When does an order become an invoice?
LEANNE: When the POD comes back.
INTERVIEWER: The signed delivery note?
LEANNE: Yes. Driver takes three copies out. Customer signs, keeps one, driver brings two back. One goes in the file, one comes to me.
INTERVIEWER: When do they come back?
LEANNE: End of the driver's shift, in a wallet. Except the ones that don't. Ivan?
IVAN: Some of them sit in the cab. I've found PODs a fortnight old under a seat.
LEANNE: And multi-drop runs, sometimes a POD gets left with the customer by mistake, both copies.
INTERVIEWER: What do you do then?
LEANNE: I ring the customer and ask them to send me a photo of theirs. Or I invoice off the picking note and hope.
INTERVIEWER: What are you looking for on the POD?
LEANNE: Anything written on it. Short by two cases, refused, wrong product, damaged. If the driver's written something I have to work out what to do with the invoice before I raise it.
INTERVIEWER: How long does that take?
LEANNE: If it's clean, seconds - I mark the order as delivered in Sage and it invoices. If there's writing on it, could be a day, because I've got to talk to the sales desk and sometimes to Ivan and sometimes to the customer.
INTERVIEWER: How many have writing on?
LEANNE: A quarter? More on a Monday.
INTERVIEWER: When do invoices actually go out?
LEANNE: I do a run every afternoon of everything cleared that day. So a Monday delivery might invoice Monday, or it might invoice Thursday if the POD's in a cab.
INTERVIEWER: Does anything check that every delivered order got invoiced?
LEANNE: Not really. There's a report I could run.
IVAN: There was that thing in February.
LEANNE: We found £11,000 of delivered orders that had never been invoiced going back four months. That was because the PODs went in the wrong tray.

recommended_improved_process: Replace paper PODs with electronic proof of delivery captured on a driver device at the point of delivery
Require structured exception reasons - short, refused, damaged, wrong product - rather than free handwriting

Report on delivery-to-invoice days and on exception volume by reason and driver

input:
LOYALTY SCHEME - MEMBER SIGN-UP
Procedure note, independent bookshop and café (single site)

The shop operates a paper-based loyalty scheme. Customers accumulate a stamp per £10 spent and receive £5 off at ten stamps. Separately, customers may join the mailing list for events and new title recommendations.

Sign-up. At the till, a customer who spends over £10 is offered a card. The card is stamped and handed over. Where the customer also wishes to join the mailing list, they complete a paper slip: name, email address, and a tick box for the categories they are interested in (fiction, children's, local history, events).

Slips are placed in a tin behind the till.

Data entry. On Sunday afternoons the owner's son, who is sixteen, types the slips from the tin into Mailchimp. He is paid for two hours a week to do this and other jobs. He types the email address, the first name and, where legible, the category ticks as tags.

Slips are then kept in a shoebox in the office.

Points recorded during the review:
- Handwriting is frequently illegible; the son estimated that he cannot read "one in six or seven" email addresses and skips those slips. The customer is not contacted.
- The paper slip carries no wording about how the data will be used and no consent statement beyond the tick boxes.
- Sign-ups made during the week are not in Mailchimp until the following week at the earliest, and longer when the son is away. Customers who signed up for an event have missed the announcement of that event.
- No welcome email is sent.
- The stamp card and the mailing list are unconnected; the shop cannot tell what a mailing list member has bought.
- The shop uses a Square till. Square holds customer records for card payments. This is not used and staff were not aware of it.
- Nobody removes unsubscribes or bounces from the shoebox, so a slip may be re-typed if it resurfaces.

gold.trigger: A customer spends over £10 at the till and is offered a loyalty card, and where they also wish to join the mailing list, completes a paper slip.

Subject: the corporate tabs

Hi Nia,

You asked about our account customers. There are about twelve local businesses - two law firms, the estate agents, a couple of building sites - who eat here and "put it on the account".

How they become an account customer: someone senior asks me if they can, and I say yes. That's it. No form, no credit check, no letter, nothing signed. I write the company name in the back of the reservations book and tell the staff.

At the end of the night the server writes the table total on a docket with the company name on it and spikes it. Once a month I gather the spikes, add them up on a calculator, and email an invoice from Sage.

Problems: dockets go missing, so some meals never get billed. Nobody's agreed who at the company is allowed to sign, so we've had a junior run up £300 on drinks and the firm refused it. Terms have never been stated - I say 30 days, they pay when they pay. The building site one owes us since February and I don't chase because I see them in here.

I don't know what any account is worth or what's outstanding without going through Sage.

Tom

Discovery notes - DTC skincare brand moving into wholesale

Present: founder (Nadia), ops coordinator (Beth)

- Wholesale is now ~30% of revenue. 60ish stockists, mostly independent pharmacies and salons, a few small chains.
- Trigger: a shop emails hello@ or fills in the "stock us" form on the Shopify site. Sometimes they DM Instagram and Nadia forwards it.
- Beth replies with a PDF line sheet and the minimum order value. If they want to proceed she sets them up.
- "Setting up" = creating a customer record in Shopify with a wholesale price tier, and adding a row to a Google Sheet called Stockist Master.
- No credit check of any kind. Beth said she "looks at the website to see if they seem real".
- Terms offered are 30 days from invoice. Beth confirmed this is offered to every new account regardless of size or history.
- No signed trading terms. No agreement on minimum resale price, territory or online marketplace restrictions - Nadia said this has already caused a problem with one stockist listing on Amazon.
- No check that the business is VAT registered or that the delivery address matches the trading address.
- First order is picked and shipped by the 3PL before payment.
- Two accounts have gone bad in the last year, roughly £4,300 written off between them.
- Nobody reviews accounts after opening. The Stockist Master sheet has stockists on it that closed down.
- Xero is used for invoicing. Stockist records in Xero and Shopify are created separately and do not always match.

CLIENT IDENTIFICATION AND VERIFICATION
Extract, practice compliance folder

Requirement: the firm must verify the identity of new clients and beneficial owners before acting, and keep records of the verification undertaken.

Current practice as described:

- Identity documents are requested from the client. Usually a passport or driving licence and a recent utility bill or bank statement.
- Documents are provided in person at the first meeting, by email attachment, or by photograph.
- Where documents are provided in person they are photocopied. Where provided electronically they are saved as received.
- Copies are placed in a folder on the shared network drive. The folder structure is by client name.
- The documents are looked at by the person who collected them.
- Electronic verification is not used. Sanctions and PEP screening is not routinely performed.
- Risk assessment of the client and the matter: not documented.
- No record is kept of the date the check was performed or by whom.
- No refresh cycle is applied to existing clients.

Observations: the shared drive folder contains documents dating back several years, including some for clients no longer acted for. Several folders contain a passport image but no proof of address. It was not possible to establish from the folder alone whether a check had been completed or merely started. Nobody was able to state who has overall responsibility for this, beyond "whoever brings the client in".

NEW CLIENT PROCEDURE
Salon operations manual, section 3 (colour and chemical services)

3.1 Every new client attending for a colour or chemical service must complete a consultation record and, where required, an allergy alert test not less than 48 hours before the service.

3.2 Responsibility. The salon manager is responsible for ensuring that a consultation record exists for every new client and for filing the record. Consultation records are completed and filed by the salon manager at the point the appointment is made.

3.3 Responsibility (as described by staff at review). The stylist performing the service completes the consultation record with the client in the chair immediately before the service begins, and files it themselves in the card box afterwards. The salon manager stated at review that she does not see consultation records and has never filed one, and that reception is not involved. Both 3.2 and 3.3 were given as the current arrangement by different staff and no version has been withdrawn.

3.4 Content of the record. Client contact details, GP details where relevant, previous chemical services, known allergies, scalp condition, and the client's signature.

3.5 Allergy alert test. Applied behind the ear or in the crook of the elbow at a separate appointment 48 hours prior. The result is read by the client at home and reported by phone or in person.

3.6 Storage. Records are held on card in the index box at reception, filed by surname.

3.7 Booking. Appointments are held in Fresha. Fresha holds no field for consultation or test status.

3.8 Where no record can be found for a client who states they have attended before, the service proceeds and a new card is started.

Subject: referencing

Hi,

You wanted to know about referencing tenants before they move in. I'll be honest, it's the bit I like least and it shows.

An applicant says they want the property. Then we need to check they can afford it and that they're who they say they are, and if they can't pass on income we ask for a guarantor.

The way it goes is somebody emails them a list of what we need. Payslips, bank statements, employer contact, previous landlord contact, ID. Then we wait. Then we chase. Then we chase again.

The guarantor form is a paper thing that has to be signed and witnessed so it gets posted out, and posted back, and half the time it comes back missing a page or the witness bit is blank.

We ring the employer if we can get a human. Sometimes we get an HR line that won't confirm anything. Sometimes we just take the payslips at face value.

Previous landlord - we email them. Some reply, plenty don't. If they don't we move on anyway if everything else looks alright.

I couldn't tell you how long the whole thing takes on average. Feels like ten days but it's been three weeks. The landlord's usually asking where we are.

I don't know who's meant to own it end to end. It kind of gets picked up by whoever's not busy, and then that person goes on holiday.

Nothing's tracked. There's no checklist that says what we've got and what's outstanding, so we ask people for things twice.

We've had one where the move-in date came and the guarantor form still wasn't back and we let them in anyway.

Let me know what you think.

gold.objective: Reference prospective tenants before move-in, including affordability, identity and guarantor checks.
gold.trigger: An applicant says they want the property.

participants: Whoever is not busy picks it up

Employer contact

Identity documents
Signed and witnessed paper guarantor form

bottlenecks_and_risks: No checklist exists showing what has been received and what is outstanding, so applicants are asked for the same documents twice
Nobody owns the process end to end - it is picked up by whoever is not busy, and that person then goes on holiday
Guarantor forms posted both ways come back missing a page or with the witness section blank, restarting the cycle

input:
Subject: opening trade accounts - my honest view

Peter,

Right, new accounts. You asked and here it is.

We're a builders' merchant and plumbing supplies wholesaler, mainly selling to small contractors and a few housebuilders. New account requests come in constantly - a bloke walks up to the trade counter and says he wants an account, or a contractor rings the sales office, or one of the reps signs someone up out on the road.

The form is a paper one on the counter. Company name, address, contact, VAT number if they've got one, two trade references, and a bank. Some of it gets filled in, most of the time the references are left blank because they can't remember any.

The form goes to Gary, our sales director. He looks at it and writes a credit limit on the top in pen. His method is - and I'm not exaggerating - whether he's heard of them and whether he likes the look of them. Twenty years in the trade, he'd say his instinct is better than any credit agency, and to be fair he's often right.

We do have a Creditsafe subscription. It's used maybe one time in ten, usually when Gary's not sure.

Once Gary's signed it, the counter staff set them up on Sage 200 with the limit, and 30 days end of month terms, same as everyone gets. They can trade immediately, often the same visit.

Nobody reviews limits afterwards. We've got accounts on £10,000 limits that were set in 2016 for people who now buy £200 a year, and lads on £2,000 who should be on £20,000.

Bad debt last year was £47,000, most of it from two groundworks firms that went under within a month of each other. Both had been on the ledger for years.

There's no stop list that works automatically. Sage will warn if they're over limit but the counter can override it and they do, because the customer's standing there.

Steve

[WhatsApp, tutoring business - owner to consultant, voice notes transcribed]

So, new students. A parent finds us, usually from a Facebook group recommendation or the website, and they message the business WhatsApp.

I reply, we go back and forth about what year the child's in, what subject, where they're struggling, what school. Sometimes that takes a week because parents message at eleven at night and I reply the next day and then they reply two days later.

Then I set up an initial assessment. It's a free 45 minute session where a tutor sits with the child, does a diagnostic on paper, and gets a feel for where they are. I have to find a tutor who's free and who does that subject, which means messaging tutors individually until someone says yes.

The assessment happens, the tutor tells me how it went - usually by voice note or in the tutor group chat - and I ring the parent and recommend a plan. So many sessions a week, which tutor, what we'll focus on.

Then if they're in, I add them to the Google Sheet, add the sessions to the calendar, and send them a Stripe link for the first month.

Things that go wrong. Parents go cold between the assessment and the plan call, and I don't chase them properly. The diagnostic paper sometimes never gets scanned so when we review progress in three months we've got nothing to compare to. I've had two where the tutor who did the assessment isn't the tutor who teaches them and the new tutor starts from scratch. And the safeguarding side - I don't take any emergency contact or medical info at intake, we just start.

We use WhatsApp, Google Sheets, Google Calendar and Stripe. Nothing joined up.

Notes - independent hardware and DIY store, 6,000 SKUs, single site

Process reviewed: stock counting and replenishment.

- EPOS is Vend. It holds a stock quantity for every SKU. Owner (Marion) and the supervisor both said the quantities are "miles out" and neither uses them for ordering.
- Reasons offered for the drift: goods receipted in bulk rather than by line, timber and fixings sold by weight or by the metre and not always scanned, staff selling loose items by keying a generic "sundries" button, and shrinkage.
- The actual count process: the supervisor (Kelly) and one other person walk the shop on Sunday afternoons with a clipboard and a printed list of about 200 lines - the fast movers and anything they know they've been short of.
- They write the counted quantity next to each line. The sheet goes into the office.
- On Monday, Marion works through the sheet and decides what to order. Her decision uses the count, what she can see on the shelves, and what she remembers selling.
- The counted figures are not entered back into Vend. So Vend stays wrong.
- Which 200 lines are on the printed list has not changed in over a year. Lines that were added to the range since are not on it.
- Slow-moving stock is never counted. Marion estimated the shop holds "a couple of years" of some lines.
- No stock value is known between annual accounts. The year-end figure is produced by a full count over the New Year weekend by family members.
- Last year's count produced a £14,000 adjustment against the book value.
- Nothing links the count to purchase ordering: orders are placed to three suppliers by different routes and no order record is compared to the count.

CLINICAL CONSUMABLES
Note in practice operations folder

Items covered: gloves, masks, aprons, matrix bands, burs, local anaesthetic, impression material, composite, bonding agents, cotton wool rolls, suction tips, decontamination pouches, and similar.

Ordering is initiated when a nurse notices that stock of an item is low or has run out. There is no minimum stock level for any item, no count, and no order schedule.

Where an item is noticed, it is either written on a pad kept in the sterilisation room or mentioned verbally. Items mentioned verbally are frequently not ordered.

Orders are placed with one of the dental suppliers. It was not established which supplier is used for which items, whether there is a preferred supplier, or who places the orders - the answer given was "whoever's got a minute". No record of orders placed was available.

Deliveries are unpacked by the nurse who finds the box. Stock is put in the store cupboard, in the surgeries, or in the decontamination room depending on what it is and where there is room. Older stock is not brought forward.

It was not possible to establish what the practice spends on consumables in a month, whether prices are compared between suppliers, whether the practice is on any pricing agreement, or what stock is currently held.

Consequences described: emergency purchases from a pharmacy or another practice; one occasion in the last year where a list was cancelled because a material had run out; and expired local anaesthetic found in a drawer during a separate exercise. Expiry dates are not checked on any routine basis.

Nobody was named as responsible for consumables.

Subject: the merch cupboard

Hi,

Something you'll enjoy. We have a cupboard.

Part of what we do for clients is branded stuff. Tote bags for a festival client, water bottles for a gym chain, notebooks and pens for conference stands, hoodies for a launch. We source it, we get it printed, we bill the client with a margin, and then whatever's left over comes back here.

Nobody manages it. It goes in the cupboard on the second floor. That cupboard now has - I counted roughly - eleven boxes, plus loose stuff on the shelves, plus a rail of hoodies in three sizes for a client we no longer work with.

We don't know what's in there, whose it is, or what it cost. Some of it is client property. Genuinely - the festival client paid for 2,000 totes, we shipped 1,600 to the event, and about 400 are in our cupboard and have been for two years. They've never asked. I'm not sure we've ever told them.

The problem shows up in a few ways. We reorder things we already have. We had to do a rush order on branded pens at four times the price for a stand in March, and there were pens in the cupboard, wrong colour but pens. Also when a client asks "how many did we have left over", we make something up.

There's no record of any of it. Orders go to the printer by email, invoices come to Ruth, and the stock just appears in the building.

I don't know what the insurance position is either, or whether we should be holding client property at all.

We use Xero and Asana. Neither has anything to do with this.

Marcus

Subject: ordering stuff

Hi,

The consumables side. Cleaning chemicals, blue roll, toilet rolls, hand soap, sanitiser for the wipe-down stations, bin bags, plus the pro-shop bits - shakers, protein bars, resistance bands.

[Voice note transcribed - owner to office admin]

Right, so you asked me to explain how the van stock works. Honestly it doesn't really "work", it just happens.

Each of the three lads has a van. They're supposed to keep the standard stuff on there - 15 and 22 mil copper, compression fittings, service valves, a couple of pumps, flexis, PTFE, the usual. Nobody wrote a list of what "standard" means, it's just what they think they need.

What happens is they get to a job, they open the drawer, and the part's not there. So they get back in the van and drive to City Plumbing on the ring road, or Wolseley if it's a Bosch part, put it on the account, and drive back. That's forty minutes minimum with the traffic and the customer's sat there watching the clock. Danny did it twice in one day last week on the same boiler.

The merchant emails us the account statement at the end of the month and that's the first time I see what's actually been bought. Then I've got to work out which job each line went to so we can bill it. Half the time the lads can't remember.

We don't have any system for this. There's no stock list, nothing on the phone. I've got a spreadsheet somewhere from two years ago with reorder levels on it that I never kept up.

Trigger is basically "we've run out mid-job". That's the whole process.

Consultant call notes - 4-partner accountancy practice, ~600 clients

Topic: retention and retrieval of archived client records.

- Practice keeps physical records: signed accounts, statutory books, older working papers, some original client documents (wills held for a handful of clients, deeds).
- Trigger for archiving: a job is finalised and the file is closed, or a client leaves.
- Current handling: papers go into a standard archive box. A member of staff writes on the end of the box in marker - typically a client name or two and a year, sometimes just a year.
- Boxes go to a self-storage unit on the industrial estate. There is no index, register or spreadsheet of box contents. Nobody could say how many boxes there are; estimate was "two hundred and something".
- Retrieval: someone drives to the unit and looks. Recent retrievals have taken over an hour; one file was never found and had to be reconstructed from the client's own copies.
- Trigger for retrieval: HMRC enquiry, a client request, or a new accountant asking for handover papers.
- No destruction schedule is applied. Boxes from the 1990s are still there. Retention policy exists in the office manual (7 years) but is not enforced against the storage unit.
- Storage unit costs £2,880 a year and has increased twice.
- GDPR: nobody can currently say what personal data is held in the unit or for whom.
- Digital files are on a server and are separately backed up; the two are not cross-referenced.

input:
Notes from stock walkthrough - salon, colour room

- Colour is the biggest consumable cost. Two brands carried: one for permanent tints, one for balayage/lightening. Roughly 300 tube SKUs plus developers, bond builders, toners.
- Ordering trigger: the colour technician (Sasha) or whichever stylist opens the last tube of a shade tells the manager, or writes it on a magnetic list on the colour room fridge.
- Manager (Denise) phones the order through to the wholesaler's rep, usually Tuesday. Rep also visits monthly and "tops up" what he thinks is needed.
- No physical count is done. Denise described it as "you look at the wall and you can see what's thin".
- Before Christmas and before the summer, Denise deliberately over-orders "so we don't get caught out". She said the last January stock take (done once, by her, on paper) found around £2,600 of colour on the shelves, against a monthly colour spend of about £1,900.
- Some tubes found were discontinued shades and out of date. These were binned.
- No link between what is used on a client and what is ordered. Fresha records the service (e.g. "full head tint") but not the grams of product used.
- Stylists mix in the colour room and any unused mixed colour is thrown away. Denise estimated "a fair bit" of waste but has never measured it.
- Retail shampoo/conditioner stock is ordered on the same call but counted separately by the receptionist, on paper.
- Wholesaler offers a portal with order history. Denise has a login but has never used it.

INVENTORY AND CHECK-IN
Departmental note, residential lettings

At the start of a tenancy an inventory and schedule of condition is prepared for the property, and the incoming tenant is checked in.

As currently carried out:

The inventory is written by hand onto a pre-printed pad, room by room, describing items and their condition. Meter readings are noted at the back. Photographs are taken on a mobile phone.

The tenant signs the pad at check-in where they are present. Where the tenant is not present, the pad is posted or the tenant is asked to sign later.

The pad copy is brought back to the office. It is understood to be filed, though it was not established where, or by whom, or whether photographs are transferred off the phone at any point.

At the end of the tenancy a check-out is carried out and compared against the inventory in order to justify any deduction from the deposit.

Points noted: it was not possible to establish which phone the photographs from recent check-ins are held on, or whether that phone belongs to the firm. The handwriting on several pads reviewed was not legible. Some pads have no meter readings. There is no standard wording for describing condition, so "good", "fair" and "some marks" are used interchangeably by different staff. No date is recorded on some pads. It is unclear what triggers the check-in being scheduled or who arranges it.

input:
WAREHOUSE PICKING AND LOCATIONS
Operational description prepared for the incoming operations manager

Site: single 14,000 sq ft warehouse, ambient and chilled, approximately 1,100 active SKUs.

Locations. The warehouse is not formally racked into addressable locations. There are no bin labels, aisle numbers or location codes. Stock is put away where there is space, with an informal convention that fast movers sit near the despatch door.

Knowledge. Where a given product is held is known by two warehouse operatives, Dave and Milan, who between them have 31 years' service. Neither has written any of it down. The stock system (Sage 200) holds quantities but has no location field populated.

Put-away. On goods in, the operative decides where a pallet goes. No record of the decision is made.

Picking. Pick notes are printed by the transport supervisor from Sage in the afternoon, listing product code, description and quantity, in product code order. The picker walks the warehouse and finds the items from memory. New starters and agency staff shadow Dave or Milan.

Consequences observed. Picking times for agency staff are roughly triple those of the two experienced operatives. Items are frequently reported as "not in stock" by a picker when Sage shows stock, and are later found elsewhere in the building. Both operatives are routinely called back from breaks and from holiday by phone. Neither is on the rota for the same day off.

Stock counts. A full count is done once a year over a weekend, with a large adjustment posted afterwards. The last adjustment was a net write-down of approximately £31,000.

Subject: past papers, workbooks, the cupboard

Hi Sam,

Materials. This is more of a problem than it sounds.

Every student on a GCSE or A-level course gets a printed workbook - we've got our own, we had them printed by a place in Leicester, plus we run through past papers and mark schemes constantly. Physical copies, because the kids work on paper for the exam so they should practise on paper.

Everything lives in a cupboard in the back room at the centre. Tutors take what they need before a session. Nobody signs anything out.

The way we reorder is: a tutor opens the cupboard, finds there are no year 11 higher maths workbooks left, and messages me. By then we're out. The printer needs ten working days and a minimum run of 50. So for those ten days tutors are photocopying at the library or emailing PDFs to parents to print, which parents hate and which looks cheap.

Past papers we print ourselves on the office printer. We've got a Ricoh on a lease with a per-copy cost. Nobody tracks who prints what. The bill was £480 one month in April which I'm certain was mostly one tutor printing whole papers in colour.

I order the workbooks by emailing the printer. I don't have a minimum stock level. I just guess based on how many students I think we'll have, and I always guess wrong in one direction or the other. We had 60 spare Year 10 English ones from last year that are now out of date because the spec changed.

I don't know what we've got in the cupboard right now. Nobody's counted it since we moved in.

Ade

Discovery notes - independent restaurant, 62 covers, no groups over 12

Process: taking and managing table reservations.

Channels in use:
- Telephone. Answered by whoever is nearest, front of house or the bar.
- The website, which has a booking widget provided by a reservations platform. Bookings from here land in the platform and email the restaurant address.
- Walk-ins.
- Instagram and Facebook messages, occasionally.
- A handful of regulars who text the owner directly.

Recording. Phone bookings are written into a paper reservations book kept on the host stand, one page per service. Widget bookings sit in the platform. Nobody transcribes one into the other in a consistent direction: staff described "copying the online ones into the book in the morning", but this was not done on either of the two days observed.

Capacity. There is no table plan in the platform. Cover limits per service are decided by the front of house manager based on how many staff are on. The widget is set to a fixed number of covers per 30 minutes and this setting has not been changed in over a year, including for December.

Confirmation and reminders. The platform sends an automated confirmation and a reminder for its own bookings. Phone bookings receive nothing.

No-shows. Estimated at 8-12 covers on a Saturday. Not recorded. No deposit or card capture on standard bookings.

Special requests. Allergies, high chairs, birthdays and access needs are written in the margin of the book or in the platform's notes field. The kitchen sees neither until service.

Reporting. Covers are counted from the till at the end of service. Bookings versus walk-ins, no-show rate and channel mix are not measured.

PERSONAL TRAINING - SESSION BOOKING
Note prepared during operations review, independent health club

Personal training is delivered by six self-employed trainers who rent floor time from the club and keep their own client fees. The club takes a monthly rent from each trainer.

Booking arrangements as they stand:

Each trainer books their own clients. Five of the six use the calendar app on their personal phone. One uses a paper diary. Two also use a separate booking app they pay for themselves, which is not connected to anything the club operates.

Clients contact the trainer directly, usually by WhatsApp or text. The club has no visibility of any PT booking.

Floor space and equipment are not reserved. Where two trainers have booked clients into the same slot, both use the gym floor at the same time. During peak evening periods this has led to members complaining that the free weights area is fully occupied by paid sessions.

The studio can be booked by trainers for one-to-one work by writing on a paper sheet pinned to the studio door. The sheet is not always honoured because class instructors do not check it.

Cancellations and no-shows are between the trainer and their client. The club is not informed.

Consequences recorded: the club cannot state how many PT sessions take place on its premises, at what times, or with how many distinct clients. When a member asks the front desk to be put in touch with a trainer, staff give out a mobile number from a list on the wall, which is out of date - two trainers on it have left. Where a member is injured during a PT session, the club has no record that the session was taking place. Insurance and PAR-Q status of PT clients who are not club members is unknown.

Subject: shoots

Hi,

You asked about how we organise photoshoots. I'll try.

We do maybe eight or nine content shoots a year - new product launches, the Christmas campaign, refresh shots when something's looking tired.

A shoot needs a photographer, a studio or a location, a stylist sometimes, models sometimes, a makeup person if there are models, products in hand, props, and someone from us there.

It's all email. Long, long email chains. Someone suggests a date, the photographer says he's got that week but not the Tuesday, the studio's got Wednesday but only a half day, the model agency comes back with options three days later by which point the studio's gone. Then it starts again.

Then when it's finally locked there's another chain about the shot list, and another about the products, and another about call times.

I honestly couldn't tell you who owns it. It's not one person. Sometimes it's me, sometimes whoever's doing the marketing at the time, and we've had two people booking things in parallel more than once.

We don't use a project tool for it. Everything's in email and some of it is in people's heads.

Things that have gone wrong: samples arriving after the shoot day. A studio booked but no photographer. Paying a cancellation fee because nobody told the model agency the date moved. Shooting products in the old packaging.

I don't know what a shoot costs us. The invoices come in over about two months from six different people and by then I've stopped counting.

There's no brief document either, so the photographer sort of makes it up and then we're surprised.

Sorry this is vague. It's genuinely like this.

Subject: the diary situation

Hi,

You asked me to write down how jobs get booked. Fair warning, my wife and I gave you different answers on Thursday and we've since had a row about it, so I'll try and put both.

My version: I take the calls, because it's my mobile on the van. If I'm under a sink I let it go to voicemail and ring back at dinner. When I've got a job I ring Amy at the office and she puts it in the diary. So the booking is mine, she's just writing it down.

Amy's version, which she wants me to include: she takes most of the calls because the office landline is on the website too and people ring that, and she books them straight into the diary herself without asking me, because if she waited for me nothing would ever get booked. She says she's been doing it that way for two years.

We're both right about our own bit and both wrong about the other's, I think. The problem is the diary. It's a big paper week-to-view on the office desk. If she books something in it, and I book something in my head on site, I don't find out about hers until I ring her, and she doesn't find out about mine until I remember. Twice this month I've turned up at a job that had been moved.

There's also no way to see how long a job needs. Everything gets written on one line whether it's a tap washer or a full bathroom.

Emergency call-outs get squeezed in and push everything back, and then Amy's ringing round apologising.

We tried a diary app about three years ago. It lasted a fortnight because I never opened it on site.

We're on QuickBooks for invoices and that's it.

Gareth

[Email thread summary provided by the office manager]

Q: How do year-end meetings get booked?

A: The partner decides they want to see a client - usually once the accounts are drafted, sometimes because the client has chased.

The partner asks one of us to "get Mr Whoever in". We email the client with two or three dates. The client replies days later, often suggesting a different date. We check with the partner, who by then has booked something else. So we go again.

I would say four or five emails per meeting is normal. Some take a fortnight to land.

There's no shared calendar that we can all see properly - the partners keep their own Outlook and two of them don't accept invitations, they just write it in a paper diary. So we're never certain a slot is actually free.

I don't know how many of these we do. It's most of January to March, and again around September.

Nobody's really in charge of it. Whoever the partner asks.

Sometimes the client turns up and the partner's out. That's happened twice this year that I know of.

[Consultant transcript - salon owner, 20 mins]

OWNER (Priya): We take bookings three ways and that's the whole problem.
CONSULTANT: Go on.
PRIYA: There's the phone - the girl on the desk writes it into Phorest, that's our salon software. There's Instagram, people DM us "have you got Saturday", and that goes to whoever's got the phone that day. And then there's people who just walk in and book at the desk.
CONSULTANT: Does the Instagram one end up in Phorest?
PRIYA: It should. Sometimes it doesn't. Sometimes it goes in as a note and not an actual appointment. Sometimes two people answer the same DM and we've told her two different times.
CONSULTANT: What starts the whole thing?
PRIYA: The client getting in touch. Or us - we're meant to rebook people at the till before they leave but that only happens maybe half the time.
CONSULTANT: Who owns the diary?
PRIYA: Me ultimately, but day to day it's Chloe on reception, and the stylists all move their own columns around in Phorest when they want a break.
CONSULTANT: Confirmations?
PRIYA: Phorest sends an SMS reminder 24 hours before, that bit's automatic. But if the booking never made it into Phorest, no reminder, and they no-show.
CONSULTANT: Colour appointments need anything extra?
PRIYA: Patch test 48 hours before if it's a new colour client. We're supposed to check. We ask them on the phone.
CONSULTANT: Recorded anywhere?
PRIYA: On a card in the box at the desk.
CONSULTANT: No-show rate?
PRIYA: I'd guess two or three a day. We don't measure it.
