input:
Discovery session notes - lettings branch, 3 negotiators + branch manager

Process reviewed: booking and conducting viewings on available rental properties.

- Trigger: applicant enquiry, mostly from Rightmove leads landing in a shared inbox, plus phone calls and walk-ins.
- Negotiator picks up the lead, phones the applicant, agrees a time verbally.
- The appointment is entered into a shared Outlook calendar used by the whole branch.
- All three negotiators book into the same calendar. Nobody blocks out travel time. Double-bookings happen "most weeks" - two negotiators arriving at the same property, or one negotiator booked at two properties across town 15 minutes apart.
- Key management is separate: keys hang on a board in the back office with a paper signing-out sheet. The sheet is often not filled in, so a negotiator arrives at a property without keys.
- Access arrangements vary: vacant properties are key-access; tenanted properties need 24 hours' notice to the tenant, which is given by phone by whoever booked it. This is not recorded, so it cannot be evidenced if a tenant complains.
- Feedback after a viewing is supposed to be phoned to the landlord within 24 hours. Branch manager (Ranjit) confirmed this happens for "maybe half" of viewings and is not logged in their CRM (Reapit) unless the applicant makes an offer.
- No-shows by applicants are common; nothing is recorded and the applicant is usually rebooked without question.
- No confirmation message is sent to the applicant after booking.

gold.objective: Book and conduct viewings on available rental properties, and feed back to landlords.
gold.trigger: An applicant enquiry arrives, mostly as a Rightmove lead in the shared inbox, plus phone calls and walk-ins.
inputs_data_required: Rightmove lead details
Applicant's agreed viewing time
Property keys and the key signing-out sheet
24 hours' notice to the tenant for tenanted properties
current_process: Applicant enquiry arrives via the shared inbox, phone or walk-in
A negotiator picks up the lead, phones the applicant and agrees a time verbally
The appointment is entered into the shared Outlook calendar used by the whole branch
Keys are taken from the board in the back office and signed out on a paper sheet
For tenanted properties, 24 hours' notice is given to the tenant by phone by whoever booked it
Feedback is meant to be phoned to the landlord within 24 hours, and is logged in Reapit only if the applicant makes an offer
bottlenecks_and_risks: All three negotiators book into one calendar with no travel time blocked, producing double-bookings most weeks - two negotiators at one property, or one booked across town 15 minutes apart
The key signing-out sheet is often not completed, so negotiators arrive at properties without keys
Tenant notice is given verbally and not recorded, so the firm cannot evidence it if a tenant complains about access
Landlord feedback happens for only about half of viewings and is unlogged unless an offer follows, so landlords are unsighted on interest
No confirmation message is sent to the applicant, and applicant no-shows are common, unrecorded and rebooked without question
recommended_improved_process: Book viewings through Reapit with per-negotiator diaries, property location and automatic travel time
Send the applicant an automated confirmation and a reminder before the viewing
Record tenant notice against the property with a timestamp when it is issued
Move key management to a logged key system requiring sign-out before a viewing can be marked ready

Report weekly on viewings held, no-show rate, feedback completion and offer conversion
ai_agent_steps: An AI agent can propose viewing slots that respect each negotiator's diary, property location and travel time, avoiding double-bookings
An AI agent can send applicant confirmations and reminders and flag likely no-shows for a call
An AI agent can issue and timestamp the 24 hour tenant access notice for tenanted properties

human_approvals_controls: A negotiator confirms the proposed slot with the applicant before it is booked
The negotiator writes or approves the viewing feedback before it is sent to the landlord
Keys must be signed out by a named person; the system records but does not release them
Ranjit reviews the weekly viewings and feedback completion report

input:
Operations review notes - regional foodservice distributor, 9 vehicles

Scope: how delivery slots are agreed and routes built.

- Customers are pubs, cafés, care homes and two small school caterers. Around 240 active accounts.
- Trigger: customer places an order (phone to the sales desk, or email, a few by fax still). At the point of order the sales desk agrees a delivery day and, if pushed, a rough time - "morning" or "before 11".
- These promises are written on the order pad and typed into the order screen as a free-text note. There is no time-slot field.
- At about 4pm the transport supervisor (Ivan) prints all orders for the next day and sorts them into piles by rough geography, from memory of the area.
- He builds the runs by hand on a whiteboard - vehicle, drops in order, driver name.
- Constraints he holds in his head: which customers can't take a 7.5-tonne vehicle, which have delivery windows because of school hours or care home mealtimes, which need a tail lift, who won't accept goods after 2pm.
- Ivan has 22 years' service. He was off for two weeks last year and the runs were, in his words, "carnage".
- Drivers phone Ivan from the road when a drop can't be made. He rearranges verbally.
- No route optimisation software. No tracking. Customers ring the sales desk to ask where the van is and the sales desk rings Ivan.
- Fuel and mileage are reviewed monthly against a budget; drops per vehicle are not measured.
- Failed deliveries are recorded on the paper POD as "not delivered" with a reason written by the driver, if he writes one.

gold.objective: Agree delivery slots with customers and build next-day vehicle runs for a regional foodservice distributor with 9 vehicles.
gold.trigger: A customer places an order by phone, email or fax with the sales desk, at which point a delivery day and rough time are agreed.

owner_and_participants.owner: Ivan, the transport supervisor (runs); the sales desk agrees the slots
participants: Around 240 active customer accounts (pubs, cafés, care homes, two school caterers)

inputs_data_required: Customer order and agreed delivery day
Rough time promised, written as a free-text note on the order
Printed orders for the next day
Ivan's knowledge of vehicle restrictions, delivery windows, tail lift needs and cut-off times
systems_involved: Order screen (free-text note field; no time-slot field)
Whiteboard used to build the runs
current_process: Customer places an order by phone, email or fax with the sales desk
The sales desk agrees a delivery day and, if pushed, a rough time such as 'morning' or 'before 11'
Promises are written on the order pad and typed into the order screen as a free-text note; there is no time-slot field
At about 4pm Ivan prints all next-day orders and sorts them into piles by rough geography from memory
He builds the runs by hand on a whiteboard - vehicle, drops in order, driver name
Drivers phone Ivan from the road when a drop cannot be made and he rearranges verbally
Failed deliveries are recorded on the paper POD with a reason if the driver writes one
bottlenecks_and_risks: All routing constraints - which customers cannot take a 7.5-tonne vehicle, school and care home windows, tail lift needs, who will not accept after 2pm - exist only in Ivan's head after 22 years, and his two-week absence produced what he called carnage
Time promises are free text on the order with no time-slot field, so they cannot be checked against the built run or reported on
Runs are built by hand with no optimisation, so vehicle and mileage efficiency is unknown and unmanaged
There is no tracking, so customers ring the sales desk who ring Ivan, adding an interruption loop to every enquiry
Drops per vehicle are not measured, only fuel and mileage against budget, so productivity cannot be improved
Failed delivery reasons depend on whether the driver chooses to write one
recommended_improved_process: Add structured delivery window fields to the order screen and capture the promise at order entry
Record customer delivery constraints (vehicle size, access, windows, tail lift, cut-off) on the customer master record
Introduce route planning software that builds runs from orders plus the recorded constraints
Give drivers electronic proof of delivery with mandatory reason codes for failed drops
Provide customers with tracking or an ETA notification to remove status calls
Measure drops per vehicle, on-time delivery against the promised window, and failed deliveries by reason
Document Ivan's constraint knowledge onto the customer master as a priority before further absence
ai_agent_steps: An AI agent can build the proposed next-day runs from orders, recorded constraints and vehicle availability, for the supervisor to approve
An AI agent can extract routing constraints from historical delivery notes and Ivan's input to populate the customer master records
An AI agent can send customers ETA notifications and proactive alerts when a drop will miss its window
An AI agent can report on drops per vehicle, on-time performance and failed deliveries by reason code
human_approvals_controls: Ivan or the transport supervisor reviews and approves the proposed runs before they are released to drivers

input:
LESSON RESCHEDULING
Note held in the business's operations document, private tuition service

Parents and students request changes to booked lessons. Requests are made by text message to a mobile number that is published on the website and on invoices.

The messages arrive at any hour, including late evening and weekends. There is no stated cut-off, notice period or cancellation charge, although the website mentions "24 hours where possible".

On receipt, the request is passed to the tutor concerned so that a new time can be found. Where a new time is agreed, the change is made in the calendar. Where it cannot be, the lesson is either cancelled or carried forward.

Records: the messages themselves are the only record of the request. Whether a lesson was rescheduled, cancelled, charged or credited is decided at the time. It was not possible to establish, from the material provided, how many lessons are rescheduled in a typical month, what proportion are charged, or whether the tutor is paid where a student cancels late.

Impact reported: tutors have travelled to a lesson that had been cancelled by text some hours earlier. Two tutors have raised that they are not paid for late cancellations, but no policy on this was produced. Invoices are queried by parents who believe they were charged for a lesson they cancelled.

gold.objective: Handle parents' and students' requests to reschedule booked tuition lessons.
gold.trigger: A parent or student sends a text message requesting a change to a booked lesson.
inputs_data_required: The text message requesting the change
The tutor's availability for a replacement slot
The calendar entry for the booked lesson
systems_involved: A published mobile number receiving text messages
A calendar in which changes are made
current_process: A parent or student texts the published mobile number to request a change, at any hour including late evening and weekends
The request is passed to the tutor concerned so that a new time can be found
Where a new time is agreed, the change is made in the calendar
Where it cannot be, the lesson is either cancelled or carried forward
Whether the lesson was rescheduled, cancelled, charged or credited is decided at the time
bottlenecks_and_risks: There is no stated cut-off, notice period or cancellation charge beyond a vague website mention of '24 hours where possible', so there is nothing to enforce
The text messages are the only record of the request, so charging decisions cannot be evidenced when a parent queries an invoice
Tutors have travelled to lessons cancelled by text some hours earlier, wasting their time and travel
Two tutors have raised that they are not paid for late cancellations but no policy on this was produced, so tutor pay is arbitrary
Requests arriving at any hour on a personal-style mobile create an always-on burden with no defined response time
It could not be established how many lessons are rescheduled monthly, what proportion are charged, or whether tutors are paid - so the commercial impact is invisible
recommended_improved_process: Publish a written rescheduling policy with a notice cut-off, charging rules and tutor payment rules
Take reschedule requests through a booking system or form rather than free-text messages to a mobile
Apply the charging rule automatically based on notice given, with the reason recorded
Notify the tutor immediately of any cancellation so no wasted travel occurs
Record every request, the notice given, the outcome and the charge against the student record
Report monthly on reschedule volume, late cancellations by student, and charges applied
ai_agent_steps: An AI agent can acknowledge reschedule requests immediately, apply the published notice rule and state whether a charge applies
An AI agent can propose replacement slots from the tutor's availability and confirm the agreed time
An AI agent can notify the affected tutor of a cancellation immediately so travel is avoided
An AI agent can produce the monthly reschedule and late-cancellation reporting
human_approvals_controls: The business owner approves the written rescheduling and charging policy
Any waiver of a late cancellation charge requires the owner's approval, recorded with a reason
A tutor confirms availability before a proposed replacement slot is committed
Disputes over a charged lesson are resolved by a person

input:
Subject: our "customer service" (using the term loosely)

Hi Nia,

Right, you wanted to know how we handle customer questions. Here's the truth.

We're a plant shop and we do a lot on Instagram - probably a third of our sales start as a DM. So questions come in through the DMs constantly. "Is this in stock", "will this survive in a north facing bathroom", "did my order go out", "can you hold one for me till Saturday".

Then there's the shop email which goes to a shared Gmail that me, Ellie and Tom can all see. And people ring the shop, and people ask in person.

Who answers? Whoever's got a minute. If I'm at the till and it's quiet I'll do a few DMs. Ellie does them on the bus in the morning. Tom does them when he's supposed to be repotting. So the same customer can get three different answers, and I have literally seen us hold the same monstera for two different people.

Nothing's marked as answered. Gmail is a mess, nobody archives, we've got 4,000 unread. Instagram at least shows you unread but if someone opens it and doesn't reply it looks done.

We don't know how fast we reply. On a busy Saturday I'd guess some DMs sit for two days.

The "will it survive" ones are the good ones - those turn into sales if you answer properly. Those are the ones that get missed most because they take longer to write.

We use Shopify for the website and Square in store. Neither is connected to the DMs obviously.

I think we're losing sales but I can't prove it.

Soph

gold.objective: Answer customer questions arriving through Instagram DMs, a shared Gmail inbox, phone and in person at an independent plant shop.
gold.trigger: A customer asks a question - by Instagram DM, email, phone or in person.
inputs_data_required: The customer's question - stock availability, plant care suitability, order despatch status, requests to hold an item
Knowledge of stock and plant care
current_process: Customers ask questions by Instagram DM, to the shared Gmail, by phone, or in person
Whoever has a minute answers - Soph between till customers, Ellie on the bus in the morning, Tom while repotting
Nothing is marked as answered; Gmail is not archived and holds around 4,000 unread
Instagram shows unread status, but an opened and unanswered message appears handled
Neither Shopify nor Square is connected to the DMs
bottlenecks_and_risks: Roughly a third of sales start as an Instagram DM, so the least controlled channel carries the most revenue
The same customer can receive three different answers from three people, and the same monstera has been held for two different customers
Opening a DM without replying makes it look handled, so messages are silently dropped
The shared Gmail has 4,000 unread with no archiving, so there is no way to tell what is outstanding
Response time is unmeasured; on a busy Saturday some DMs are estimated to sit for two days
The high-value 'will it survive in my bathroom' questions take longest to answer and are the ones most often missed, so the losses fall on the most convertible enquiries
recommended_improved_process: Bring all channels into one shared inbox tool with assignment and status
Assign a named owner per shift rather than whoever has a minute
Record holds and reservations against the item so the same plant cannot be promised twice
Build a short set of saved replies for the most common care and stock questions
Set and measure a response time target, with a separate target for care advice enquiries
Publish a care guide and stock availability on the Shopify site to deflect routine questions

An AI agent can triage incoming messages across channels, tagging them by type and routing them to the shift owner
An AI agent can flag messages opened but not replied to, and messages approaching the response time target
An AI agent can report on response times, volume by channel and enquiry type
human_approvals_controls: The shift owner reviews and sends AI-drafted replies rather than sending automatically
A person confirms and records any hold or reservation on stock
Soph approves the published care guide content and any pricing or availability commitment
Complaints and refund requests are handled by a person, not by the automated triage

input:
[Reception desk observation and interview - GP practice, 8,400 patients]

INTERVIEWER: A patient rings with a question for a doctor. What happens?
SUE (reception): Depends what it is. If it's a result, I'll look and see if it's been filed with a comment. If there's a comment I read it out.
INTERVIEWER: And if not?
SUE: I write it on a sticky note. Name, date of birth, what they want, their number, and which doctor.
INTERVIEWER: Then?
SUE: The notes go on the doctor's pigeonhole shelf, or if it's urgent-ish I'll walk it through between patients and put it on their desk.
INTERVIEWER: How many a day?
SUE: Thirty? Forty on a Monday.
INTERVIEWER: Do they all get answered?
SUE: Most. Dr Fenwick is very good, he does them at the end of surgery. One or two of the others, the notes build up.
INTERVIEWER: How do you know if a patient has been rung back?
SUE: We don't. The patient rings again and says nobody called, and then I write another sticky note.
INTERVIEWER: Do you put anything in the clinical system?
SUE: EMIS? Only if it becomes an appointment. The query itself doesn't go anywhere.
INTERVIEWER: What about notes that get lost?
SUE: They fall off. They go in the bin with the paper. It happens.
INTERVIEWER: Any way of knowing how long a query has been waiting?
SUE: No. There's no date on them half the time.
INTERVIEWER: Who's responsible for making sure they're all cleared?
SUE: Nobody really. The practice manager asks about it now and then.
INTERVIEWER: Complaints from this?
SUE: Yes. "I rang three times." That's the main one.

gold.objective: Handle patients' telephone queries for a GP practice with 8,400 patients, from the call to a clinician's response.
gold.trigger: A patient rings the practice with a question for a doctor.
inputs_data_required: The patient's name, date of birth, query and telephone number
Which doctor the query is for
Filed results with a clinician's comment, where one exists
systems_involved: EMIS (clinical system; the query itself is not recorded in it)
current_process: A patient rings with a question for a doctor
For a result, reception checks whether it has been filed with a comment and reads the comment out
Otherwise reception writes the patient's name, date of birth, query and number on a sticky note along with the doctor's name
Notes go on the doctor's pigeonhole shelf, or are walked through to the desk between patients if urgent-ish
Doctors deal with them at their own pace - Dr Fenwick at the end of surgery, others allowing notes to build up
The query itself is not entered into EMIS unless it becomes an appointment
bottlenecks_and_risks: Thirty to forty queries a day, up to forty on Mondays, are handled on sticky notes that physically fall off and go in the bin with the paper
There is no way to know whether a patient has been called back - reception finds out only when the patient rings again, and writes another sticky note
Many notes carry no date, so there is no way to tell how long a query has been waiting
Nobody is responsible for ensuring queries are cleared; the practice manager asks about it now and then
Response depends entirely on individual doctors' habits, so the same query gets very different service depending who it is for
The query never enters EMIS, so there is no clinical record that the patient made contact
The most common complaint is 'I rang three times', which is the direct output of this design
recommended_improved_process: Record every telephone query as a task in EMIS against the patient record, with date, time and receiving clinician
Set a response time target and make outstanding tasks visible to clinicians and the practice manager
Route queries by type - results, medication, administrative - rather than all to a named doctor
Require the clinician to close the task with the outcome, creating a record that the patient was contacted
Give reception visibility of open and closed tasks so a patient calling back can be told the position
Report weekly on query volume, response times and overdue tasks
ai_agent_steps: An AI agent can capture the query into a structured EMIS task from the reception call, including patient identifiers
An AI agent can route queries by type to the correct clinician or administrative queue
An AI agent can escalate tasks approaching or breaching the response time target to the practice manager
An AI agent can produce the weekly volume, response time and overdue task report
human_approvals_controls: A clinician answers every clinical query and closes the task with the outcome; the AI does not answer clinical questions
Reception confirms the captured query with the patient before it is submitted
The practice manager reviews overdue and escalated tasks
Any query indicating urgency is escalated to a clinician immediately by a person

input:
[Kitchen pass, mid-afternoon - two conversations, transcribed]

INTERVIEWER: If someone rings up about allergies, what happens?
LIV (front of house): Whoever picks up the phone deals with it. We know the menu.
INTERVIEWER: Is there something you read from?
LIV: There's the allergen matrix in the folder by the till. It's a printout.
INTERVIEWER: When was it last updated?
LIV: I don't know, chef does it.
[Later, with the head chef]
INTERVIEWER: The allergen matrix - who maintains it?
CHEF (Marek): Front of house do it. They print it off from the supplier data. It's their document, they own it, I don't touch it.
INTERVIEWER: Liv said you do it.
MAREK: No. I tell them if a dish changes. What they do with that is up to them.
INTERVIEWER: Do you tell them every time a dish changes?
MAREK: If I remember. We change the specials daily.
INTERVIEWER: Are the specials on the matrix?
MAREK: No, the specials aren't on it. You'd have to ask the kitchen.
INTERVIEWER: And if someone rings at 3pm and asks about a special?
MAREK: Front of house would come and ask us.
INTERVIEWER: Liv, would you?
LIV: If someone's in the kitchen, yeah. Between two and four there might not be.
INTERVIEWER: What do you say then?
LIV: I'd say I'll ring them back. I might forget.
INTERVIEWER: Is anything written down when a guest tells you their allergy?
LIV: On the booking, as a note. If they booked online there's a box.
MAREK: We don't see the booking notes in the kitchen. We get told on the night by the waiter.
INTERVIEWER: Always?
MAREK: Should be. Not always.

gold.objective: Answer customers' allergy queries by telephone and get allergen information to the kitchen and to the table.
gold.trigger: A customer telephones to ask about allergens, or tells front of house their allergy on the night.

owner_and_participants.owner: Contradictory in input: Liv says the chef maintains the allergen matrix, while Marek says front of house own it and he does not touch it - each attributes ownership of the same document to the other
participants: Liv and other front of house staff

inputs_data_required: The printed allergen matrix in the folder by the till, derived from supplier data
Booking notes where a customer recorded an allergy online
Verbal information from the kitchen about specials
systems_involved: An online booking system with an allergy notes box
A printed allergen matrix in a folder by the till
current_process: A customer telephones about allergens and whoever picks up the phone deals with it
The member of staff reads from the printed allergen matrix in the folder by the till
Specials, which change daily, are not on the matrix, so front of house go and ask the kitchen
Between two and four there may be nobody in the kitchen, in which case the customer is told they will be rung back
Where a customer states an allergy on a booking it is recorded as a note, including via a box on the online booking form
The kitchen does not see booking notes and is told on the night by the waiter
bottlenecks_and_risks: Ownership of the allergen matrix is contradictory and unresolved - front of house believe the chef maintains it, the chef believes front of house own it - so a life-safety document has no actual owner and its update date is unknown
The chef tells front of house when a dish changes only 'if I remember', while specials change daily, so the matrix is knowingly incomplete
Specials are not on the matrix at all, so the highest-churn menu items have no documented allergen information
Between two and four nobody may be in the kitchen, so the customer is promised a call back that Liv acknowledges she might forget
The kitchen does not see booking allergy notes and relies on the waiter telling them on the night, which the chef says should always happen but does not
Any member of staff answers allergy calls with no training requirement or script
recommended_improved_process: Assign a single named owner - the head chef - for the allergen matrix, with a required update whenever a dish or special changes
Include specials on the matrix as part of writing the special
Hold allergen information in a system accessible to both front of house and the kitchen rather than a printed folder
Flow booking allergy notes through to the kitchen ticket automatically
Define who may answer allergy calls and give them a script, including what to do when the kitchen is unavailable
Require the kitchen to acknowledge each allergy on a table before service

Workshop notes - agency client services, "how work arrives"

- Retained clients, 19 of them, each with an account manager.
- Work arrives from clients through: shared Slack Connect channels (12 clients), email to the account manager, email to a general address, phone calls to the account manager's mobile, and comments left directly on designs in Figma.
- There is no ticketing system. Asana holds planned project work but not incoming requests.

- Requests made in a Slack channel while the account manager is on leave are frequently missed. There is no cover convention.
- Volume unknown. Nobody has counted requests. Estimate offered was "maybe 200 a week across the agency".
- Time spent on these small requests is not recorded against the client, so retainer profitability excludes it.
- Two clients have complained in the last quarter about things "falling through the cracks".

CUSTOMER ORDER ENQUIRIES
Process description, coffee subscription and roastery

Volume: approximately 2,400 active subscriptions plus one-off orders. Enquiry volume estimated at 120-180 emails per week, rising sharply after any despatch delay.

Enquiry types, by rough share: order not arrived or late (the majority), subscription changes (skip, pause, change grind, change frequency), address changes, grinder and brew advice, wholesale enquiries misdirected to the consumer address.

Trigger: customer emails the support address, replies to a despatch notification, or messages the brand's Instagram.

Handling: all email is answered by a virtual assistant, Marilou, who works from the Philippines. Her working hours overlap with UK mornings only. She works from Gmail, using the shared support mailbox.

To answer a "where is my order" enquiry Marilou must look in three places: the subscription platform to see whether an order was generated and when, the roastery's despatch spreadsheet which the packing team fill in daily, and the courier's tracking site. The despatch spreadsheet is often a day or two behind.

Where she cannot resolve an enquiry she flags it by moving the email to a Gmail label called "For Katie". Katie is the founder. This label currently holds 60+ emails, some several weeks old.

Subscription changes are made by Marilou directly in the platform.

Refunds and replacement sends require Katie's approval, requested by WhatsApp message. Katie approves these while doing other things, usually in the evening.

Not measured: response time, resolution time, volume by type, repeat contacts. There is no help centre or FAQ page. No macros or saved replies are used; every answer is typed.

input:
CUSTOMER CONTACT AND CALL HANDLING
Written note, plumbing and heating contractor

The business publishes one telephone number, which is the owner's mobile. It appears on the vans, the website, the invoices and in the local directory.

All customer contact arrives at this number: new enquiries, requests to book a job, callers chasing an engineer who has not arrived, existing customers reporting a problem with completed work, merchants, and out-of-hours emergency calls.

The owner answers where he can. He is on the tools four days a week, so calls are frequently taken while working, in a loft, or from under a bath. Where he cannot answer, the call goes to voicemail. The voicemail greeting is the standard network one and does not identify the business.

Voicemails are listened to at the end of the day, in the van, and returned in whatever order they were left. Some are not returned.

There is no call log. Missed calls are visible only in the phone's call history, which the owner reviews "when it occurs to him". Numbers that are called back and do not answer are not followed up.

Emergency calls at night are answered if the phone is heard. There is no out-of-hours arrangement, no diversion and no cover when the owner is on holiday; on the last two holidays the phone was taken abroad and answered.

Appointments arising from calls are written into the paper diary that lives in the office, so a booking taken on site must be remembered and passed on later that day. Several have not been.

No record exists of enquiry volume, conversion, or the reason for calls. The office administrator has asked twice for a business number and a shared inbox.

input:
Subject: January

Hi,

Writing this in the first week of February so it's fresh.

The shared inbox. That's the thing I want to fix.

Client queries come to a general address. In a normal month it's manageable. In January it isn't. Everybody wants to know if their return's been filed, whether they need to pay, how much, whether the payment on account is right, and whether that letter from HMRC matters.

The inbox is on Outlook and everybody in the office can see it. That's the problem - if everybody can see it, nobody's actually responsible for it. There's no rule about who picks things up. Some days two people answer the same email. Some days nothing gets answered because everyone assumes someone else has.

We don't mark things as done. There's no flag, no folder system that anyone follows. Some people move things to a folder, some don't.

I couldn't tell you how many emails came in during January. Or how long people waited. It felt like hundreds a day.

The other thing is people email the partner they know directly as well, so the same question is in two places and gets two answers.

Nobody's in charge of it. That's the honest answer to your question. Priya sort of watches it but she's got her own work.

We do have practice management software but it isn't connected to the email at all as far as I know.

Anyway. There must be a better way. What do people normally do?

Angela

Consultant call notes - tutoring agency, 14 tutors, GCSE/A-level

Subject: how parents' questions about progress are handled.

- Parents contact the business or the tutor directly. Both happen.
- Owner (Farida) stated: "All parent contact comes through me, the tutors don't deal with parents, that's the rule."
- Later in the same call, describing a specific case, Farida said tutors "obviously message parents about how the session went, that's normal, they've all got the parents' numbers."
- When this was put back to her she said both were true - the rule is that formal progress questions come to her, but "day to day chat" goes direct. There is no written definition of which is which.
- Tutors use their own phones and personal WhatsApp. Numbers are not held centrally.
- Tutors write a session note after each lesson "when they remember" into a shared Google Sheet. Completion rate estimated at 60%.
- When a parent asks "is my child improving", Farida either forwards it to the tutor, or answers from the session notes if they exist, or asks the tutor to call.
- Response time is not measured. Farida thought "same day usually", but also said messages sometimes sit over a weekend.
- No standard progress report exists. Two tutors have started sending their own half-termly write-ups; the rest send nothing.
- Complaints about lack of communication were mentioned as the most common reason for cancellations.

SEASONAL RECRUITMENT - CURRENT PRACTICE
Note prepared for the owner, independent department store (menswear, homeware, toys), 11 permanent staff

Requirement. The store takes on between 6 and 9 temporary sales assistants from late October to early January, plus one or two for the January sale.

Attraction. A handwritten card is placed in the window in early October reading "Christmas staff wanted - enquire within". The vacancy is also mentioned on the store's Facebook page in some years but not others. No job description exists.

Application. Candidates come to the counter and either hand in a CV or ask for a form. There is no form. CVs are placed in a pile behind the till. The pile is not dated. Some CVs are lost.

Selection. The owner (Hazel) goes through the pile "when it gets to a decent size", usually late October, and rings people she likes the look of. Interviews are held on the shop floor between customers and last around ten minutes. There is no list of questions and no notes are taken. Where Hazel is unavailable, the deputy manager interviews instead, using her own judgement.

Offer. Made verbally on the day or by phone. Pay rate is quoted verbally. Hours are described as "flexible, around 16-25".

Onboarding. Right to work documents are checked on the first shift, by whoever is on. Copies are photocopied and put in a drawer. Contracts are issued by the accountant "at some point", occasionally after the person has already finished. Training is shadowing an experienced colleague for one shift.

Subject: locums - I think we're being taken for a ride

Hi Mark,

You said to write down how we book locum cover so here goes, though writing it down has already made me wince.

We're a three-surgery mixed practice. When one of the associates is off - holiday, sick, maternity from March - we need a locum dentist or we cancel the list, and cancelling a list costs us about £1,400 in lost UDAs and private.

What I do is ring round. There are three agencies I use. I ring the one I spoke to last, and if they can't fill it I ring the next one, and so on. Sometimes I've got two agencies working the same date without either of them knowing, and once we ended up with two locums turning up on the same Monday, which was an expensive morning.

The rates are all over the place. One agency charges a day rate plus a fee, one takes a cut of the UDA value, and one I genuinely couldn't tell you how they bill because the invoice is a single line. I have never compared them side by side. I just take whoever can fill the gap.

Then there's the paperwork. They're supposed to send me a compliance pack - GDC registration, indemnity, DBS, hep B, ID. Some do, some send it after the locum has already worked, and one sent me a pack for a different dentist entirely. I don't have a checklist. It goes in a folder on the desktop called "Locums" and I couldn't tell you which of them is complete.

Induction is me showing them where the loo is and which computer to use. They don't know our systems (SOE and Digital Dental X-ray) so the nurse ends up driving.

Notice is usually days, sometimes hours.

I know this is bad. Where do I start?

Julie (Practice Manager)

Subject: KPs

Alright,

You asked about hiring kitchen porters. There's not much to tell.

There's a WhatsApp group with everyone who's ever worked here in the kitchen, must be forty people in it. When we're short, someone puts a message in it. "Anyone free tonight, KP, 5 till close."

Whoever replies first gets it. Sometimes nobody replies and the chefs do the pot wash themselves and the service is a nightmare.

Some of them have worked here before so we know them. Some are mates of mates and we've never met them. They turn up, they work, we pay them.

I couldn't tell you who's actually in charge of it. Whoever notices we're short, I suppose. Head chef mostly. Sometimes me.

Right to work, I know we should. Some of them we've got copies of somewhere from before.

Pay is cash sometimes if it's a one-off, or through the books if they stick around.

Turnover is brutal. I'd say we've had fifteen different KPs this year.

Nothing's written down. No rota beyond the week ahead which is on the wall.

Anyway that's it. Not much of a process I know.

Call notes - plumbing and heating contractor, use of subcontract labour

- Business runs 5 employed engineers and uses subcontract plumbers to cover peaks, typically 3-6 subbies at any time, more during boiler replacement season.
- Trigger for engaging a subbie: workload exceeds capacity, usually identified when the owner (Wayne) looks at the diary and sees jobs slipping more than two weeks out.
- Sourcing: word of mouth, a local trades Facebook group, or subbies who have worked for the firm before.
- Engagement is a phone call. Day rate agreed verbally. No written agreement, no CIS verification recorded at that point, no confirmation of what jobs they will do.
- Gas work: subbies doing gas must be Gas Safe registered. Wayne says he "asks to see the card". No copy is taken and no check is made against the Gas Safe register online. There is no record for any current subbie of their registration number or expiry.
- Public liability insurance: not requested.
- Qualifications for unvented cylinders and water regulations: not checked.
- Right to work: not checked for subbies.
- CIS: the bookkeeper verifies subbies with HMRC before the first payment, which is after they have already worked. Two have been verified at the higher rate because the details given were wrong.
- Induction: none. Subbies are given an address and a job description by phone.
- Work is not inspected before or after. Two callbacks in the last year were traced to subcontract work but the firm cannot evidence who did it because job sheets are not always signed by name.
- The firm's own insurance requires that subcontractors carry their own cover. Wayne was not aware of this condition.

input:
TRAINEE RECRUITMENT
Practice note, four-partner accountancy firm

The practice recruits one to three trainees each year, typically school leavers on an AAT pathway and graduates on an ACA training contract.

Attraction. The vacancy is placed on Indeed and on the practice website, and is sent to two local colleges and one university careers service. The advert text is reused each year with the date changed.

Application. Candidates apply with a CV and covering letter to a generic mailbox. Applications are printed by the office manager and placed in a wallet.

Sifting. Each partner takes the wallet in turn and marks the CVs. There is no scoring template. Partners variously look at grades, at whether the candidate is local, at the presentation of the letter, and at "whether they'd fit in". Marks are made in pen on the CV itself. Where two partners disagree the candidate is discussed at the partners' meeting.

Assessment. Shortlisted candidates attend an interview with two partners. There is no question set; partners ask what occurs to them. Some candidates are given a numeracy test that was written in-house some years ago; whether it is used depends on which partner is interviewing. No notes are retained.

Decision. Made at the partners' meeting, by discussion. Feedback is not given to unsuccessful candidates and rejections are frequently not sent at all.

Recording. Applications are held in the wallet until the round closes and are then shredded. No record is kept of who applied, who was interviewed, on what basis a decision was made, or of protected characteristics.

Outcome. Trainee retention past the second year is poor - four of the last seven left. Reasons are not recorded. Two partners believe the problem is the calibre of candidate; one believes it is the training given. This has not been tested.

input:
APPRENTICE RECRUITMENT
Salon procedure note

The salon takes on one or two apprentices a year on a hairdressing apprenticeship with a local training provider.

Sourcing. Apprentices come from three routes: a family member or friend of an existing member of staff; a client's son or daughter; or someone who comes in and asks. The salon does not advertise. The training provider has offered to send candidates and this has been declined in the past on the basis that "we like to know who we're getting".

Selection. The candidate is invited to do a trial day. They shadow a stylist, sweep, wash hair, make drinks, and are observed.

The trial day is unpaid.

There is no assessment form, no list of what is being looked for, and no scoring. At the end of the day the stylist they shadowed gives a verbal opinion to the manager. The opinion is typically expressed as whether the candidate is "good with people", "willing", or "a bit quiet".

Decision. Made by the manager, sometimes the same day. Offered verbally.

Paperwork. The training provider handles the apprenticeship agreement and the funding. The salon signs what it is sent. A contract of employment is issued by the salon's payroll provider, sometimes several weeks after the start date. Right to work checks are made by the payroll provider from documents the salon photographs and emails on.

Subject: hiring negotiators

Hi,

Following on. You asked how we recruit lettings negotiators.

We're always hiring, is the honest answer, because they don't stay. Two left in the last six months and one of those had been here seven weeks.

The way it happens is somebody leaves, and then we need someone quickly because the patch isn't covered, so we put something on Indeed. The advert's an old one we keep reusing.

CVs come in. Someone goes through them - it varies who. Then we get people in for a chat.

The chat is exactly that. Twenty minutes, in the meeting room, usually with whoever's free. There's no set of questions. We ask them about themselves and about the area and whether they've got a car. If we like them we offer.

I couldn't tell you what we're actually looking for. If you asked three of us we'd say different things. One of us thinks it's all about attitude, one thinks you need someone who's sold something before.

We don't take notes. We don't score. We don't have a second stage. I don't think we've ever had two people in on the same day so we could compare.

References - we say we take them. I'm not certain we always do.

Then they start and there isn't really an induction. They shadow someone for a day and then they're on the phones.

I don't know what it costs us when one leaves. Someone worked it out once and it was a big number.

I don't know who owns this. HR is me and I'm not HR.

Ranjit

[Voice note transcribed - tutoring business owner]

How I recruit tutors. Someone messages me, usually off a Facebook post I put in a local teachers' group, or a current tutor recommends a friend.

I have a chat with them on the phone, twenty minutes. I ask what they teach, what boards, whether they've taught the new spec, and whether they've got a DBS.

If they seem good, I ask for their DBS certificate, two references and a photo of a qualification. I put those in a Gmail folder called "Tutor onboarding". Some of them are in that folder, some are still sitting in my inbox because I never moved them.

Then I add them to the tutor WhatsApp group and start sending them students.

What I don't do: I don't check the references properly, I just note that they came. I don't do a trial lesson, which I think is a mistake because two people have been terrible and I've had to move students. I don't check the DBS is on the update service so I can't verify it's still valid.

There's no contract. They're self-employed and there's nothing signed.

Farida

Notes - discovery call, family homeware & gift shop (2 stores)

Attendees: owner (Marion), shop supervisor (Kelly). 45 mins.

- Reordering is entirely driven by the sales rep from their main giftware supplier. He visits every second Tuesday.
- Marion: "Ivan comes in, we walk round the shelves together, he writes what we need on his pad, and that's the order."
- Marion later said the reorder is "Kelly's job now, I've handed that over completely, she does it."
- Kelly, when asked directly, said she has never placed an order and only tells Ivan what has sold out on the shelf she's responsible for.
- No purchase order raised. No written confirmation. Order arrives 10-14 days later with a delivery note.
- Delivery note is checked against the boxes (not against any order record, because there isn't one). Discrepancies written on the note in biro.
- Note goes in a box file. Invoice arrives separately by post, matched to the note "when Marion gets round to it".
- EPOS (Vend) does hold stock quantities but Marion said the counts are "miles out" and nobody uses them for ordering.
- If something sells out between visits it stays out of stock for up to a fortnight unless Marion phones Ivan personally.
- Two other suppliers (candles, cards) are ordered online by Marion at home.
- No minimum stock levels defined anywhere.
- Christmas ordering is done in July from the same rep, from memory of last year.

LABORATORY WORK PROCEDURE
Section 7 of practice operations manual, dental practice (3 surgeries)

7.1 Purpose. To describe the current handling of work sent to and returned from external dental laboratories (crowns, bridges, dentures, orthodontic appliances).

7.2 Initiation. A clinician determines at the chairside that laboratory work is required and completes a paper laboratory prescription. The impression or scan and the prescription are placed in the collection box in the sterilisation room.

7.3 Despatch. The laboratory courier attends on Tuesdays and Fridays. The nurse on duty hands over the box and records the item in the courier's duplicate docket book, entering the patient's surname, the item and the date.

7.4 Tracking during manufacture. No record is maintained by the practice other than the docket book entry. The expected return date is agreed verbally with the courier or laboratory.

7.5 Return. Completed work is delivered by the same courier and signed for by whoever is at reception. Work is placed in the cupboard in surgery 1 filed by patient surname.

7.6 Fitting. The patient's fit appointment will already have been booked at the time of the impression, typically two to three weeks ahead.

7.7 Known issues recorded at last review: work not returned in time for the booked fit appointment is discovered on the morning of the appointment; there is no proactive check. Two laboratories are used and it is not always clear from the docket book which holds an item. Laboratory invoices are checked against the docket book only when the amount looks unusual.

gold.trigger: A clinician determines at the chairside that laboratory work is required (crown, bridge, denture or orthodontic appliance).

Laboratory invoices

input:
Subject: freelancers and POs - it's got away from us

Hey,

Picking up from Thursday. You asked how we book freelancers so here's the honest version.

We use maybe 25-30 freelancers regularly. Motion designers, copywriters, a couple of devs, video editors, and a photographer we use constantly. Plus new ones when a job needs something weird.

The way it works is a producer or an account director realises they need someone, opens Slack or WhatsApp, and messages a freelancer directly. "Are you free Tues-Thurs, we need 3 days on the Halcyon edit." Freelancer says yes. That's the booking. Sometimes there's a day rate in the message, sometimes there isn't because we've used them before and everyone assumes it's the same rate as last time. It often isn't - a few have quietly put their rates up and we find out on the invoice.

The PO gets raised afterwards, if it gets raised. Our finance person (Ruth) creates it in Xero when the invoice arrives so it can be coded to a project. So the PO is basically a post-rationalisation.

Problems this causes: we've had two freelancers booked for the same job by two different producers. We've had a freelancer do 5 days when the client only approved 3, and we ate the difference. Nobody knows total freelance spend by client until Ruth does the month end, and even then it's only as good as the project code someone typed.

There's no rate card, no contract, no NDA on most of them, and no check on whether they've got their own insurance. The photographer's been working for us for four years on nothing but WhatsApp messages.

We're on Xero and Asana and Slack. Asana has the projects but not the bookings.

What would you do first?

Marcus

[Call recording extract - founder and operations lead]

CONSULTANT: Your bestseller went out of stock for seven weeks. Walk me back to how that order gets placed.
NADIA: So the factory is in Portugal for the base and the fill is done here. The Portugal side is the long one, ninety days from PO to landing.
CONSULTANT: What triggers you raising the PO?
NADIA: Me looking at the stock number in Shopify and going "ooh, that's getting low".
CONSULTANT: When do you look?
NADIA: When I think of it. Or when Beth says something.
CONSULTANT: Is there a reorder point set anywhere?
NADIA: No. There's a tab in the Stockist Master sheet where I once worked out cover in weeks but it's from last year.
CONSULTANT: How do you decide the quantity?
NADIA: Honestly? What we ordered last time, plus a bit if it's been selling well. Round it up to a full pallet because the freight's better.
CONSULTANT: Do you factor in the wholesale pipeline?
NADIA: No. That's the thing - wholesale orders land in lumps. A chain took 900 units in one go in March and that's what wiped us out.
CONSULTANT: Does anyone see the wholesale pipeline?
NADIA: Beth knows who's talking to us but it's in her head and in email.
CONSULTANT: Once the PO's raised?
NADIA: I email the factory. They confirm, they send a proforma, I pay 30% deposit, then 70% before shipping. It comes by road, we clear it, it goes to the 3PL.
CONSULTANT: Do you track it in between?
NADIA: The freight forwarder emails updates. They sit in my inbox.
CONSULTANT: If it slips?
NADIA: I find out when I chase, usually because we're already low.

Discovery notes - accountancy practice, IT and software spend

- Practice runs a lot of software: tax and accounts production, practice management, payroll, bookkeeping, e-signature, a CRM nobody uses, cloud storage, two AI tools bought last year, plus Microsoft 365.
- Every one of these renews annually on a card. Most are on the managing partner's personal business credit card.
- Trigger for renewal: none. They auto-renew. The first anyone knows is the card statement or the receipt email.
- No renewal calendar. No list of what the practice subscribes to. The office manager (Wendy) was asked to produce one during the review and could not complete it - she found four subscriptions nobody could account for.
- Seat counts are not reviewed. Three departed staff still have licensed seats on the tax software, at £780 a seat.
- Price increases are not challenged. The practice management system went up 22% at last renewal and this was noticed three months later.
- Nobody negotiates. Nobody checks whether the tier is right - they are on the top tier of the bookkeeping product and use two of its features.
- Coding in the accounts is inconsistent, so total software spend is not visible on the P&L in one place. Estimated at "£30k-ish" by the managing partner; the actual figure was not available during the review.
- Data processing agreements: not held for any of the tools. This matters because client data sits in most of them.
- Two tools overlap almost entirely in function and were bought by different partners.

input:
CONTRACTOR INSTRUCTION AND WORKS ORDERS
Extract, property management department procedures

Where a repair is required at a managed property, a contractor is instructed to attend.

Section 4.1 (as written). All works are instructed by means of a works order raised in the property management system. The works order carries a unique number, the property address, the reported fault, the access arrangements, the agreed limit of expenditure and the landlord's authorisation reference. No contractor may attend without a works order number. The property manager for the block raises and issues the order.

Section 4.2 (added at a later date, author not recorded). In practice repairs are instructed by telephone. The maintenance coordinator calls a contractor from the approved list, describes the fault and asks them to attend. Job numbers are not issued. The system is updated afterwards where time allows. The property manager is not involved in day-to-day repairs; this sits with the maintenance coordinator.

Both sections remain in the current procedures folder and staff cited each of them during the review as describing what is done.

Further observations. Contractors invoice with a description and an address but no reference, so invoices are matched by hand to whatever record exists. Where no record exists the invoice is queried with the maintenance coordinator, who works from memory. Limits of expenditure are stated verbally on the call, if at all; three invoices in the last quarter exceeded the landlord's standing authority and were paid. Access arrangements and tenant contact details are given verbally. Where a contractor cannot gain access, the abortive call charge is passed to the landlord without evidence of what was arranged. Completion is confirmed by the contractor's invoice arriving; no separate confirmation is sought from the tenant.

gold.trigger: A repair is required at a managed property.

input:
PURCHASING AND REPLENISHMENT
Description of current process, wholesale distributor (ambient, chilled, non-food)

Range: approximately 1,100 active SKUs across 60 suppliers.

Tool. A single Excel workbook, "Buying Sheet", maintained by the purchasing manager. One row per SKU with columns for minimum stock, maximum stock, case size, supplier, lead time and last cost.

Maintenance. The minimum and maximum figures are reviewed quarterly, in principle. In practice the last full review was over a year ago. Some rows still carry minimums set for lines that have since been delisted by their supplier.

Cycle. Each Monday the purchasing manager exports current stock quantities from Sage 200, pastes them into the Buying Sheet, and reads down the sheet for lines below minimum. She raises purchase orders per supplier by email.

Judgement applied outside the sheet: promotions agreed by the sales team, seasonal uplift, a supplier's minimum order value that makes it worth adding lines, and rumours of price increases. None of this is written down.

Not used by the sheet: forward orders already taken from customers, sales trend or seasonality beyond memory, supplier reliability, or shelf life on chilled lines.

Consequences recorded: out-of-stocks on around 40 lines in a typical week, measured only when the sales desk complains. Overstocks on chilled lines resulting in waste - £18,000 written off last year. Two suppliers require 12 weeks lead time; the sheet's lead time column shows 4 for both, and this has caused repeated gaps.

Goods receipting is done against the delivery note by the warehouse and entered into Sage by the office; the purchase order is not always matched, so price differences between order and invoice are found only when the invoice is queried, which is rare.

Purchasing performance - service level, stock turn, days of cover - is not measured.

input:
Subject: past papers, licences and the printer bill

Hi Sam,

Another one for the list. Materials again but the buying side rather than the cupboard.

Three things we buy: past paper and mark scheme access from the exam boards (some is free on their sites, some needs a centre login or a licence), workbooks from the printer in Leicester, and the actual printing which is on our Ricoh lease.

Nobody owns any of this. What happens is a tutor needs something and either buys it themselves and claims it back, or messages me and I buy it, or just uses whatever's in the cupboard.

The claiming back is the bit that's got out of hand. Tutors send me photos of receipts on WhatsApp. Some of them are for things I'd never have approved - one bought a full set of revision guides for a single student at £14 each. I pay them because it feels petty not to, and because they've already spent the money.

The exam board stuff - I genuinely don't know what we're licensed for. I know one board wants you to be a registered centre to get some materials, and I know at least one tutor is downloading things from a site that I suspect isn't legitimate. I've not asked, which probably tells you something.

Copyright is the bit that worries me. We photocopy published workbooks. I don't know if we're allowed. Nobody's ever checked.

The Ricoh is per copy, mono and colour different rates. The bill varies from £120 to nearly £500 a month and I can't explain the difference. There's no code, anyone can print.

I buy the workbooks by emailing the printer, no PO, and the invoice comes 30 days later.

Ade

input:
[Coffee shop, informal - owner of a homeware shop, recorded]

CONSULTANT: How do you find out when a customer's unhappy?
MARION: Google, usually.
CONSULTANT: Meaning?
MARION: A review appears. One star. And I read it and think, oh, that was three weeks ago and nobody told me.
CONSULTANT: So they don't complain in the shop?
MARION: Some do. But that gets dealt with by whoever's on and I don't hear about it.
CONSULTANT: Dealt with how?
MARION: Depends. A refund, or a swap, or an apology.
CONSULTANT: Is that recorded?
MARION: No.
CONSULTANT: When a review does appear, what do you do?
MARION: I reply to it. Sometimes. If I'm annoyed I leave it a few days.
CONSULTANT: Do you contact the customer?
MARION: I can't usually. You don't get their details from a review.
CONSULTANT: What proportion do you reply to?
MARION: I couldn't say. Not all of them.
CONSULTANT: Email complaints?
MARION: They go to the shop address. I look at that most days.
CONSULTANT: Who else looks at it?
MARION: Just me I think.
CONSULTANT: How many complaints would you say you get a month?
MARION: Honestly no idea. Two? Ten? I don't count.
CONSULTANT: Are there themes?
MARION: Deliveries. The furniture deliveries, definitely. That's the courier not us but they don't care.
CONSULTANT: Has that been raised with the courier?
MARION: I've mentioned it.
CONSULTANT: Is there a point where something comes to you automatically?
MARION: No. It's if someone tells me.
CONSULTANT: Do staff know what they're allowed to do to put something right?
MARION: They'd ask me. Or they'd guess.

Discovery notes - dental practice, complaints (two interviews)

- Asked how a patient complaint is handled.
- Practice manager (Julie): "Everything comes to me. I write it in the complaints log, I acknowledge within three working days, and the principal signs off the response. It's all in the log, that's how we do it."
- Practice principal (Mr Achebe), separately: "Most of them never get as far as a log. A patient grumbles at the desk, the manager sorts it there and then, and quite rightly. The log is for the serious ones - the ones that mention the GDC or a solicitor. There'd be three or four a year in there."
- Both stated theirs was the current practice.
- The complaints log was produced. Four entries for the last twelve months, all with solicitor or regulator involvement. The most recent acknowledgement letter on file was sent eleven working days after the complaint.
- Reception staff described "two or three a week" that are resolved verbally - waiting times, a charge the patient did not expect, a receptionist's manner.
- These are not recorded anywhere and are not seen by the practice manager unless she is at the desk.
- No theme analysis. No complaints item on the practice meeting agenda.
- The practice's published complaints procedure states a 10 working day response and names a person who left in 2022.

input:
Consultant call notes - 32 cover bistro, town centre

- Asked how complaints are handled. Answer was essentially "we sort it there and then".
- Typical: diner unhappy with a dish or a wait. Waiting staff tell the manager on shift. Manager goes to the table, apologises, takes the item off the bill or sends over drinks/dessert.
- Could not tell me who the manager on shift is on any given night - it rotates and there is no rota naming a duty manager.
- Nothing is written down. No log, no book, no note in the till system.
- Asked how they know if the same dish is generating complaints - they don't. "You'd just kind of remember."
- Asked about complaints that arrive after the visit (email, TripAdvisor, Google). Long pause. Someone "usually replies". Could not say who or how quickly.
- No definition of when something is escalated to the owner. Owner said he "hears about the bad ones".
- Kitchen is not routinely told when a complaint concerns food. Chef sometimes finds out days later.
- Value of comped items is not tracked separately on the till - it goes through as a discount with no reason code.
- No follow-up with the diner afterwards.
- Asked what triggers the process - unclear beyond "a customer says something".

input:
CLIENT SATISFACTION AND ESCALATION
Internal handbook extract - integrated marketing agency, 22 staff

The agency does not operate a formal complaints procedure. Client dissatisfaction is surfaced and dealt with as follows.

Identification. Dissatisfaction is usually first noticed by the account manager on a client, either from the tone of an email, a difficult call, or a client raising an issue in a status meeting.

Escalation. The account manager raises the client's name at the Monday morning agency standup, which is attended by the account team, the creative director and the two partners. The item is discussed verbally. Standup is time-boxed to 30 minutes and covers all accounts.

Resolution. An action is agreed in the room - typically that a partner will call the client, that additional work will be done at no charge, or that the team will "get back on top of it". Ownership of the action is assigned verbally.

Recording. No written record is made of the client's concern, the agreed action, the owner or the outcome. The standup is not minuted.

Review. Client health is not reviewed on any cycle between standups. There is no client satisfaction survey. Churn is discussed at the quarterly partners' meeting, at which point the reasons for a departure are reconstructed from memory.

Note: two of the last four accounts lost had been raised at standup at least once in the preceding quarter.

gold.objective: Surface and resolve client dissatisfaction at a 22-person integrated marketing agency.
gold.trigger: The account manager notices dissatisfaction - from the tone of an email, a difficult call, or a client raising an issue in a status meeting.
inputs_data_required: The account manager's observation of the client's tone or stated issue
Verbal discussion at the Monday standup
current_process: The account manager notices dissatisfaction from an email's tone, a difficult call, or an issue raised in a status meeting
The account manager raises the client's name at the Monday morning agency standup, attended by the account team, creative director and both partners
The item is discussed verbally within a standup time-boxed to 30 minutes covering all accounts
An action is agreed in the room - a partner will call the client, extra work will be done free, or the team will 'get back on top of it'
Ownership of the action is assigned verbally
No written record is made of the concern, action, owner or outcome; the standup is not minuted
bottlenecks_and_risks: Identification depends entirely on an account manager inferring dissatisfaction from tone, so a quietly unhappy client is never surfaced
A 30-minute standup covering all accounts leaves minutes per client, so serious issues get the same airtime as trivia
Verbally assigned actions with no written owner or deadline are not followed up, and nobody can check whether the promised call happened
Free additional work is agreed in the room with no cost attached and no approval, directly reducing account profitability
Client health is not reviewed between standups and there is no satisfaction survey, so problems are only caught once visible
Two of the last four accounts lost had been raised at standup at least once in the preceding quarter, showing the process does not prevent churn
recommended_improved_process: Log every client concern with the client, the issue, an owner, an action and a due date
Introduce a lightweight client health check on a regular cycle, not only when someone notices a problem
Define an escalation threshold at which a partner takes ownership within a set time
Cost and approve any remedial free work before it is committed to the client
Track the concern to a recorded outcome and confirm closure with the client
Review open concerns and churn risk at the partners' meeting, not only at quarterly churn post-mortems
ai_agent_steps: An AI agent can analyse client email and meeting notes for sentiment and flag accounts showing early signs of dissatisfaction
An AI agent can chase overdue actions on the concern log and escalate them at the defined threshold
An AI agent can issue and collate the periodic client health check responses
An AI agent can prepare the open-concerns and churn-risk summary for the partners' meeting
human_approvals_controls: An account manager or partner confirms any AI-flagged dissatisfaction before it is treated as a live concern
Free remedial work above an agreed value requires partner approval before it is offered to the client
A named human owner is recorded for every concern and must confirm closure
All client-facing communication about a concern is written and sent by a person

input:
MEMBER FEEDBACK AND COMPLAINTS
Extract from operations file, independent health club (1,900 members, pool, studio, gym floor)

Channels available to members. A suggestion box is mounted on the wall by the changing room corridor, with a pad of slips and a pen. Members may also speak to staff on the desk or email the club's general address.

Handling of box submissions. The box is emptied by the duty manager. There is no set frequency; the operations file records that it "should be weekly". In practice it has been emptied when it is visibly full or when the general manager asks.

Triage. Slips are read by the duty manager who emptied the box. Slips concerning cleanliness of the changing rooms or the pool - the large majority - are shown to the cleaning contractor's supervisor verbally at the next site visit. Slips concerning equipment are passed to the fitness manager. Slips concerning staff conduct are given to the general manager.

Response to the member. Slips are usually anonymous, so no response is possible. Where a member has written their name, a response is at the discretion of the manager reading it.

Recording. Slips are not logged. After action, they are binned. There is no count of how many are received, by theme, or over time.

Recurring themes noted anecdotally by staff during this review: showers running cold in the men's changing room (raised repeatedly over at least eight months), broken lockers, and the temperature of the studio.

Escalation. There is no defined point at which an issue is escalated to the owner or reviewed at management meeting. The monthly management meeting agenda does not include member feedback.

gold.objective: Collect and act on member feedback and complaints at an independent health club with 1,900 members.
gold.trigger: A member puts a slip in the suggestion box, speaks to staff on the desk, or emails the club's general address.
inputs_data_required: Slips written by members on a pad by the suggestion box
Verbal comments at the desk
Emails to the club's general address
systems_involved: A suggestion box mounted by the changing room corridor
current_process: A member writes a slip and puts it in the suggestion box, speaks to desk staff, or emails the general address
The box is emptied by the duty manager with no set frequency - the file says weekly, in practice when visibly full or when the general manager asks
Slips are read by the duty manager who emptied the box
Changing room and pool cleanliness slips, the large majority, are shown verbally to the cleaning contractor's supervisor at the next site visit
Equipment slips go to the fitness manager and staff conduct slips to the general manager
Slips are usually anonymous so no response is possible; where a member has written their name, a response is at the reading manager's discretion
After action the slips are binned and nothing is logged
bottlenecks_and_risks: Slips are binned after action and never counted, so a theme cannot be evidenced - cold showers in the men's changing room have been raised repeatedly over at least eight months without being fixed
Emptying the box only when it is visibly full means a member's issue may sit unread for weeks
Anonymous slips make response impossible, so members receive no acknowledgement and stop bothering
Passing cleanliness complaints verbally to the contractor's supervisor leaves no record and no way to hold the contract to account
There is no defined escalation point to the owner, and member feedback is not on the monthly management meeting agenda, so nothing reaches decision-makers
No count by theme or over time means the club cannot tell whether feedback is improving or worsening
recommended_improved_process: Offer a named feedback route - a QR code, app form or email - alongside the box, capturing the member's identity by default
Log every item of feedback with theme, date, member and channel
Set an emptying and triage frequency for the box with a named owner
Acknowledge every named piece of feedback within a defined time and tell the member the outcome
Raise cleanliness issues to the cleaning contractor in writing against the contract, with a response deadline
Put a member feedback item with theme counts on the monthly management meeting agenda
Define an escalation threshold at which an issue goes to the owner
ai_agent_steps: An AI agent can classify incoming feedback by theme and route it to the cleaning contractor, fitness manager or general manager automatically
An AI agent can detect a recurring theme, such as repeated cold shower reports, and escalate it once a threshold is passed
An AI agent can draft acknowledgement and outcome messages to named members for approval
An AI agent can produce the monthly theme count report for the management meeting
human_approvals_controls: A duty manager or the general manager approves the response before it is sent to a member
Escalation to the owner is confirmed by the general manager
Formal notice to the cleaning contractor under the contract is issued by a manager, not automatically
Complaints concerning staff conduct are handled by the general manager and are not auto-routed

input:
Subject: parcels arriving smashed - our "process"

Hi Rachel,

Following our call. Here's how we deal with damaged deliveries, and I'll be upfront, it's costing us a fortune.

We're a homeware brand, mostly ceramics and glassware, sold through our own Shopify site. About 400 orders a week, up to 900 in Q4. Everything ships from our unit, we pack ourselves, and we use two carriers - one for standard, one for next day.

Customer emails or messages Instagram saying it arrived broken. Usually with a photo, sometimes without.

Our customer service person, Leah, has one rule from me: refund or replace immediately, no questions, don't argue about it. So she does. She either issues a full refund in Shopify or raises a replacement order, and she replies apologising. Turnaround is usually within a couple of hours, which is genuinely good and people say nice things about it.

What we never do is claim off the carrier. Not once. There's a claims process, I know there is, and there's a window - I think it's 14 days for one of them and 28 for the other. We've never filed one. Partly because you need the photos and the packaging kept, and we tell the customer to just bin it.

We also don't record which carrier it was, which product, or which packer. So I can't tell you if it's one carrier, one product, or one person packing badly. My gut says it's the tall vases but that's a guess.

Leah keeps a rough note in a Google Sheet sometimes when she remembers.

Last month breakage refunds were about £2,700. That's straight off the bottom line.

Ben

gold.objective: Handle customer complaints about parcels of ceramics and glassware arriving damaged, and recover the cost.
gold.trigger: A customer emails or messages Instagram to say their order arrived broken, usually with a photo.

owner_and_participants.owner: Ben (the writer); Leah handles the complaints day to day
participants: Two carriers - one standard, one next day

inputs_data_required: The customer's message and photo where provided
The order in Shopify
Carrier claim requirements - photos and retained packaging
systems_involved: A Google Sheet where Leah keeps a rough note when she remembers
current_process: A customer emails or messages Instagram to report a broken item, usually with a photo
Leah issues a full refund in Shopify or raises a replacement order immediately, with no questions, under a standing instruction from Ben
Leah replies apologising, usually within a couple of hours
The customer is told to bin the damaged item and packaging
No claim is filed against the carrier
Leah keeps a rough note in a Google Sheet when she remembers
bottlenecks_and_risks: No carrier claim has ever been filed despite claim windows of around 14 and 28 days, so the full breakage cost - about £2,700 last month - falls on the business rather than the carrier
Telling customers to bin the item and packaging destroys the evidence a claim would require, making recovery impossible even retrospectively

Carrier, product and packer are not recorded, so it cannot be established whether breakages are driven by one carrier, one product or one person packing badly - Ben's suspicion about tall vases is a guess
The Google Sheet is kept only when Leah remembers, so there is no reliable data even at the level being attempted
The refund-first policy gives excellent service and good reviews but is entirely uncosted and uncontrolled
Volume rises to 900 orders a week in Q4, when the unrecovered cost will scale with it
recommended_improved_process: Capture every breakage report on a structured form recording order, product, carrier, packer and photographs
Ask the customer to retain packaging and provide photographs before the refund is issued, as a condition of the carrier claim
Keep the fast refund or replacement, but file the carrier claim in parallel within the claim window
Track claims filed, paid and rejected by carrier
Analyse breakage rate by product, carrier and packer monthly
Act on the analysis - change packaging for the worst products, or renegotiate or switch carrier
ai_agent_steps: An AI agent can capture the structured breakage record from the customer's email or Instagram message, including extracting order and product detail
An AI agent can prepare and file the carrier claim within the claim window from the captured evidence
An AI agent can produce the monthly breakage analysis by product, carrier and packer
An AI agent can draft the apology and refund confirmation to the customer for Leah to send
human_approvals_controls: Leah approves and sends the customer response; the refund decision remains with a person
Refunds or replacements above an agreed value require Ben's approval
A person reviews the carrier claim before it is submitted
Ben approves any change of carrier or packaging arising from the analysis

input:
Subject: going back to jobs for free

Hi,

You asked about callbacks - where we've done a job and we end up going back.

It happens more than I'd like. Someone rings and says the tap's dripping again, or the rad's cold, or there's a damp patch under the sink. Usually they ring my mobile.

I just send whoever's nearest. Or I go myself if I'm passing. We don't charge, obviously, because we did the original job. Takes an hour or two, sometimes half a day if it's a proper leak and there's a ceiling down.

I don't know how many we do. It's not written anywhere. It doesn't go on the job system because it's not a job, it's a return.

I couldn't tell you if it's the same lad every time or the same type of job. My gut says compression fittings on plastic pipe but I might be wrong.

We don't ask why it failed. We just fix it and go.

There's no time limit on it either. Someone rang last month about a job we did in 2022 and we went.

I don't know what it's costing us. Materials are pennies but the hours aren't.

Anyway, that's the situation. What would you look at first?
