[Transcript - salon manager, colour correction cases]

CONSULTANT: A client isn't happy with their colour. Take me through it.
DENISE: Usually they ring the next day. Or two days later once they've washed it and it's gone brassy. Sometimes they put it on Instagram first, which is worse.
CONSULTANT: Who takes the call?
DENISE: Reception. They pass it to me if I'm in, or they book the client back in themselves.
CONSULTANT: What do you offer?
DENISE: We get them back in. Free. Usually with the same stylist because I think they should fix their own work, but if the client won't have them I put them with Sasha because she's the technician and she can rescue most things.
CONSULTANT: How long does a correction take?
DENISE: A proper one? Three, four hours. Sometimes two visits. That's a whole column of a stylist's day for nothing.
CONSULTANT: Is that recorded anywhere?
DENISE: It goes in Fresha as an appointment at zero. So the stylist looks like they've had a quiet day.
CONSULTANT: Does that affect their commission?
DENISE: Yes and they hate it. That's caused a few rows.
CONSULTANT: Do you record the reason?
DENISE: No. Just "colour correction" if that.
CONSULTANT: So could you tell me which stylist generates the most?
DENISE: I could tell you from memory. I couldn't show you.
CONSULTANT: What about the original consultation - do you look back at what was agreed?
DENISE: There's a card with the formula on it. Sometimes what's on the card isn't what was actually mixed.
CONSULTANT: Does the client sign anything at the original appointment?
DENISE: No.
CONSULTANT: Refunds?
DENISE: Occasionally, if they won't come back. I'd say four or five last year. I decide those.
CONSULTANT: Above a certain value do you check with the owner?
DENISE: No, there isn't a limit.

input:
Discovery notes - distributor, claims and credits (2 sessions)

Process: handling customer claims for short deliveries, damages and incorrect items.

- Volume: significant. Sales office estimated 15-25 claims a week across ~240 accounts.
- Trigger: customer phones or emails the sales office, usually the day of or after delivery.
- Sales office practice: raise a credit note in Sage for the value claimed and post it. No investigation.
- Sales director (Gary) described the process as follows: "Anything over £100 comes to me for authorisation, always has. I see every one." He was clear that this is a firm rule.
- Sales office manager (Trish), asked the same question in a separate session, said: "We just do them. Gary doesn't see them. If we asked him for every credit we'd never get anything out." She estimated that fewer than one in twenty are referred upward.
- Both accounts were given as the current practice. Sage does not enforce an approval limit; any user in the sales office can raise and post a credit.
- No reason code is used. The narration field usually says "short" or "credit as agreed".
- No check is made against the picking note, the POD or the driver.
- No analysis is done of which customers claim most, which products are involved, or which drivers or pickers are associated.
- Warehouse are not told about claims. The picker who short-picked is not informed.
- Total credits raised last year were said to be "around £90k" but the exact figure could not be produced during the session.
- One customer has claimed on 40% of their deliveries. This was known anecdotally to the sales office and had never been escalated.

gold.trigger: A customer phones or emails the sales office, usually the day of or after delivery, to claim.

owner_and_participants.owner: Contradictory in input: Gary, the sales director, states firmly that every claim over £100 comes to him for authorisation and that he sees every one, while Trish, the sales office manager, states they simply raise them, Gary does not see them, and fewer than one in twenty are referred upward

The warehouse is not told, and the picker who short-picked is not informed
bottlenecks_and_risks: The approval control is contradictory and unresolved - the sales director believes he authorises every claim over £100, the sales office manager says fewer than one in twenty are referred and that referring them all would stop the business functioning - so it cannot be established whether any authorisation happens
Sage does not enforce an approval limit, so any user in the sales office can raise and post a credit of any value

input:
HANDLING OF PARENT CONCERNS ABOUT TUITION
Written note, tuition service

Concerns raised by parents about a tutor fall into three broad types: the tutor's approach or manner, punctuality and reliability, and lack of visible progress.

Current handling.

A parent raises a concern, usually by message or in conversation at the end of a session. The concern is received by the owner.

The owner listens and, in most cases, offers to change the child's tutor. This is framed to the parent as a matter of finding a better fit. The change is made for the following week where a tutor with the right subject and availability can be found.

The tutor who has been replaced is told that the family's circumstances have changed, or that the timetable has been rearranged. The substance of the concern is not put to them. The owner's stated reason is that tutors are self-employed, in short supply, and would be likely to stop taking work if criticised.

No record is made of the concern, the response, or the change of tutor beyond the amended entry in the calendar.

Consequences noted during the review:
- Two tutors have each been replaced on multiple families without ever being told why. Neither has had the opportunity to change their practice.

[Call transcript - practice manager and practice accountant]

ACCOUNTANT: Take me through how you work out what the associates get paid.
DEBORAH: Right. There are four associates. They're all on a percentage of what they bill, but the percentages aren't the same and the lab deduction isn't the same either.
ACCOUNTANT: Go on.
DEBORAH: Two are on 45% of gross, less 50% of the lab bill. One is on 42% but the lab comes off in full before the percentage. And Mr Achebe's son is on 50% flat with no lab deduction at all because that was the deal when he joined.
ACCOUNTANT: Where do the gross figures come from?
DEBORAH: I run a production report out of SOE per performer for the month.
ACCOUNTANT: Does that report split private and NHS?
DEBORAH: It does but the NHS side is UDAs, so I have to convert UDAs to money using the contract rate, and that's a separate calculation on my spreadsheet.
ACCOUNTANT: And the lab bills?
DEBORAH: Lab invoices come in by post and email from two labs. I go through them line by line and work out whose patient each item was, because the invoice has the patient's name but not the dentist. If I don't recognise the name I have to look it up in SOE.
ACCOUNTANT: How many lines a month?
DEBORAH: Sixty, seventy.
ACCOUNTANT: How long is the whole thing taking?
DEBORAH: Two days. I do it in the week after month end and I dread it.
ACCOUNTANT: Does anyone check it?
DEBORAH: The associates check it. Very carefully.
ACCOUNTANT: Errors?
DEBORAH: Most months one of them queries something. Usually a lab item on the wrong person. Last year I underpaid one of them by £1,100 over three months and only found it when he worked it out himself.
ACCOUNTANT: Are the percentages written down anywhere?
DEBORAH: In their associate agreements, in the filing cabinet. One of them I can't find.

Session notes - agency finance, freelancer payment cycle

- Around 30 freelancers used across a year, 12-18 active in a typical month.
- Freelancers are told to invoice monthly. Some invoice per job, some invoice monthly, two invoice quarterly and one hasn't invoiced since October.
- Invoices arrive by email to the finance address, in PDF, Word, and in one case as text in the body of an email.
- Finance assistant (Kofi) checks each invoice against what the agency believes was booked. The record of what was booked is: Slack messages, an entry in Asana if someone made one, and the producer's memory.
- Where the invoice matches, it is entered in Xero, coded to a project, and scheduled for payment on the 20th.
- Where it does not match, Kofi messages the producer who booked the freelancer. Producers are usually on client work; replies take days.
- Rates are not held anywhere central. Kofi has built his own spreadsheet of "what we paid this person last time" as a defensive measure.
- Self-billing is not used. No purchase orders are raised in advance.
- Two freelancers have been paid twice in the last year - once for a duplicate invoice with a different number, once where two producers each approved the same work.
- CIS does not apply; IR35 status determinations have not been made for any freelancer. Nobody in the agency could say whether this is required for their engagements.
- Payment is late in most months because the reconciliation isn't finished by the 20th. Freelancers chase Kofi directly, and two have declined work as a result.
- The partners see freelance cost only in the monthly management accounts, in one total line.

Call notes - gym, class instructor payment

- 11 freelance instructors, roughly 60 classes a week across studio and spin.
- Instructors are paid per class, at rates between £22 and £35 depending on how long they have been there and how well attended the class is. Rates are not written down anywhere central.
- Attendance is recorded on a paper sheet the instructor takes into the studio. Members sign in on it.
- The sheet is supposed to go into a tray in the office after the class. Many do not - they are left in the studio, taken home in an instructor's bag, or thrown away.
- At month end the duty manager on that day gathers the sheets and builds a list of classes delivered per instructor.
- Where a sheet is missing, the instructor is asked how many classes they did and that figure is used.
- The list goes to the bookkeeper who pays by bank transfer. Instructors do not invoice.
- Legend, the membership system, has class booking - members book classes in the app - but the booked list is not used for payment because "people book and don't turn up".
- Nobody reconciles classes paid for against classes actually scheduled on the timetable.
- Two instructors have been paid for classes that were cancelled for low numbers.

PROCESS NOTE - Temporary Warehouse Labour: Hours to Payment
(Internal, undated, held in Operations shared folder)

Scope: covers agency-supplied temporary pickers and packers at the fulfilment site. Does not cover permanent staff, who are on the standard monthly cycle.

Subject: RE: payroll bureau - the thing I mentioned

Morning David,

Sorry this is long. You asked about the payroll side of the practice, which is honestly the bit that keeps me awake.

We run payroll for about 40 client companies. Anything from a two-person limited company to a care home with 90 staff. It's all done by Priya and a part-timer, Wendy, who does Tuesdays and Thursdays.

The way it works: each client is supposed to send us their hours and changes before their cut-off, which is different for every client because their pay dates are different. Some are weekly, most are monthly, two are four-weekly.

What actually arrives is anything. Excel files, some of them lovely, some of them with merged cells and a total that doesn't add up. Photographs of a paper timesheet taken on a phone, at an angle. One client sends a WhatsApp voice note listing who worked what. The care home sends a PDF from their rota system that has to be retyped.

Priya keys it all into BrightPay, runs the payroll, and emails the payslips and the report back for approval. Then she waits. Some clients approve in an hour, some don't reply at all and she just submits the RTI on deadline day and hopes, because if we miss it they get the penalty and blame us.

Changes come in late constantly. Someone left three weeks ago and nobody told us until we'd already paid them. We've done four extra payroll runs this quarter to fix things like that and we don't charge for them.

Pension assessment is in BrightPay, that bit's ok. But we're re-keying the same data three times in some cases.

I've no idea what any individual payroll client actually costs us to serve. The fees were set years ago.

Any thoughts welcome.

Angela

input:
Notes - tuition business, tutor payment process

- 14 tutors, all self-employed, paid per session delivered.
- The record of sessions delivered is a shared Google Sheet. Each tutor has a tab and enters their own sessions: date, student, duration, rate.
- Tutors have edit rights to the whole sheet, not just their tab.
- Owner (Farida) stated that she checks every line against the booking calendar before payment: "Nothing gets paid that I haven't matched off."
- Business partner (Ade) stated separately that no checking takes place: "We pay what's on the sheet. There's no way to check it, the calendar's not accurate because of all the reschedules." He said this has been the case since they took on the tenth tutor.
- Both statements were given during the same session and neither was withdrawn.
- Payment run is monthly, by bank transfer, made by Farida from the business account.
- Tutors do not raise invoices. There is no self-billing document. Nothing is issued to the tutor confirming what they were paid for.
- Rates differ by tutor and by subject and are held in Farida's head and in individual email offers.
- Travel to a student's home is paid for some tutors and not others; the rule for this could not be stated.
- Sheet has no version protection. Edit history exists but is not reviewed.
- Two disputes in the past year where a tutor said they had delivered sessions that were not paid. Both were resolved by paying.
- No one reconciles what tutors are paid for against what parents were invoiced for.

gold.trigger: The monthly payment run falls due.

owner_and_participants.owner: Contradictory in input: Farida states she checks every line against the booking calendar before payment and nothing is paid unmatched, while Ade states no checking takes place and the calendar is not accurate enough to check against - both were given in the same session and neither withdrawn

input:
Subject: inspection - I don't want to do this again

Hi Mark,

We had our inspection in April. We passed, but the six weeks before it nearly finished me off and I want to describe what happened so we can stop it happening again.

The way it works is you get notice, and then you have to produce evidence against a long list of standards. Decontamination, radiography, safeguarding, complaints, staff training and registration, waste, medical emergencies, recruitment checks, patient feedback, the lot.

What we do - what we did - is nothing, until the letter arrives. Then it's panic.

Six weeks out I made a list of everything they'd ask for. Then I went hunting. Autoclave printouts were in a folder in the decon room, but three months were missing because the printer ran out of paper and nobody said. Staff CPD certificates - some in the personnel files, some in people's email, one nurse's were on a laptop that had been wiped. The radiography audit hadn't been done for two years so we did one retrospectively over a weekend, which I'm not proud of. Fire drill - we couldn't evidence one, so we did one and wrote it up. The complaints log had four entries and I know we had more than four complaints.

The medical emergency drug expiry check is supposed to be monthly. There was a sheet with signatures for January and then nothing until the week I started looking, when suddenly there were signatures for every month, and I know for a fact nobody did them.

Everything is paper, in different rooms, owned by different people, with no schedule saying who does what and when.

The one good thing is SOE holds the clinical stuff properly.

I've got three years before the next one. What should I put in place now?

Julie

gold.trigger: Currently nothing - evidence gathering starts only when the inspection notice letter arrives, roughly six weeks before the visit.

input:
Subject: the fridge logs (and everything like them)

Hi Nia,

Right, you asked me about food safety records. This is uncomfortable to write down.

We're supposed to check and record fridge and freezer temperatures twice a day, opening and close. There's a paper sheet on a clipboard in the kitchen with a grid on it - one row per unit, columns for the days. Six units: two walk-ins, three under-counters, one freezer.

What's supposed to happen is a chef probes each one at the start and at the end and writes the number in.

What happens is Friday. On a Friday, whoever's on realises the sheet is blank and fills the whole week in. And because nobody actually knows what the temperatures were, they write numbers that look right. 3, 4, 3, 2, 4. Never a 7. Never a number that would mean you'd have to do anything.

Same thing with the delivery temperature checks, and the cooking and cooling records, and the cleaning schedule sign-off. All of it, Friday.

Our HACCP pack is a folder that came from a consultant in 2019. The dishes in it aren't the dishes we cook now.

The environmental health officer came in 2022, we got a 5, and honestly I think that was because the sheets were full in. Which is exactly the problem - the records look better than the reality.

The thing that scares me is we did have a fridge fail last summer. The seal went on the under-counter one, and we lost a load of stock. Nobody had probed it for days. If somebody had been ill I'd have had a folder full of made-up numbers to hand to the EHO.

We've got an electronic till (Lightspeed), and Fourth for rotas, but nothing for this. It's all paper on clipboards.

Where would you start?

Tom

[Slack huddle notes, agency ops - typed up by the ops manager]

Topic: data protection. Prompted by a client's procurement questionnaire asking for our records of processing.

What we found:
- We have a document called "Data Processing Register.xlsx" on the shared drive. Last modified 26 months ago. It was made by an ops person who has since left.
- It lists 11 processing activities. We now do things that aren't on it at all - the whole influencer side, the CRM work we do for two clients, and the customer data we handle for the e-commerce account.
- It lists 6 sub-processors. We currently use, by my count, at least 19 tools that touch client or consumer data.
- Nobody has read it since it was written.
- We do have a privacy notice on the website. It references a company name we changed in 2023.
- Data processing agreements: we have signed DPAs with 3 clients. The other 16 have never asked and neither have we.
- We hold consumer email lists for 4 clients in our own Mailchimp account, under our billing, which I think means we're a controller for some of that and nobody has ever thought about it.
- Retention: we don't delete anything. There is client data on the drive from accounts we lost in 2019.
- Subject access requests: never had one. No process if we do.
- Breach: we had a laptop stolen from a car last year. Nothing was reported or assessed. I don't know if it was encrypted.
- Training: none.
- Nobody is the named data protection lead. Elin (managing partner) assumed I was doing it. I assumed our external IT people were.

Action from the huddle: "Priyanka to look into it." No date set.

- Business ships approximately 90,000 parcels a year plus wholesale cases. Now in scope for packaging producer obligations and pays a fee based on tonnage of packaging placed on the market.

Consultant notes - heating & gas engineering firm, 6 engineers

Process: issuing and retaining Landlord Gas Safety Records (CP12) and Building Regs notifications.

- Trigger: engineer completes an annual landlord safety check or a boiler installation.
- Engineer fills in a carbonless triplicate CP12 pad in the van. Top copy to the tenant or left at the property, second copy to the landlord/agent, third copy stays in the pad.
- Owner (Wayne) collects the pads back off the engineers "when they're full", which he estimated as every 6-8 weeks.
- Third copies are then filed in a lever arch file by month, not by property or landlord.
- Building Regs notification for new installs is done separately by Wayne on the Gas Safe Register portal, from the engineer's job sheet. He does this in a batch, usually at the weekend. Legal window is 30 days; he admitted some have been late.
- Agents regularly phone asking for a copy of a certificate for a specific address. Wayne has to go through the lever arch file by hand. Estimated 15-20 minutes per request, several requests a week.
- Some pads have been lost or left in vans that were sold. There is no other copy of those records.
- Engineers' Gas Safe registration expiry dates are held on a sheet pinned in the office.
- No reminder system for when a property's next annual check is due - relies on the agent asking.

Subject: traceability - what happens if we get a recall

Hi Peter,

You asked me to write down how we'd actually trace a batch if a supplier issued a recall, because I said on the phone that I wasn't confident. Here it is warts and all.

We're an ambient and chilled wholesaler, we do about 1,100 lines, mostly to independent convenience stores and a few caterers. Chilled is the risky bit - cooked meats, cheese, some ready meals.

Goods in: the driver hands over a delivery note, our goods-in lad checks the pallet count and the temperature with a probe, writes the temp on the note, and signs. He does NOT record lot numbers or best-before dates anywhere. They're on the cases but they don't get captured.

The stock goes into the chiller and gets put wherever there's space. First in first out is "supposed to happen" but there's no location system, so if a new pallet goes in front of an old one the old one gets picked last.

Picking: the picker works off a printed pick note per customer, ticks off what he's picked, and writes on it if he substituted something. Again no lot numbers.

So if a supplier rings tomorrow and says "recall all Batch L2274 of the sliced ham", what we can actually do is: look at the goods-in notes to find roughly when a ham delivery came in, then look at every customer who bought sliced ham in the following two weeks, and ring all of them. That's probably 80 shops for one product.

We keep the pick notes in a drawer for a few months then they get binned. Nobody's ever tested this.

We're due a BRC-style audit from one of our bigger customers in the autumn.

Steve

gold.objective: Trace an affected batch of product through goods in, storage and picking so that customers can be identified in the event of a supplier recall.
gold.trigger: A supplier issues a recall for a specific batch, for example 'recall all Batch L2274 of the sliced ham'.

participants: Around 1,100 lines of customers - independent convenience stores and caterers

inputs_data_required: Supplier delivery notes with pallet count and probed temperature written on
Printed pick notes per customer, ticked off and annotated with substitutions
Case-level lot numbers and best-before dates (present on the cases but never captured)
current_process: A delivery arrives; the goods-in operative checks the pallet count, probes the temperature, writes the temperature on the delivery note and signs
Lot numbers and best-before dates are not recorded anywhere, although they are printed on the cases
Stock goes into the chiller wherever there is space, with no location system, so a new pallet placed in front of an old one causes the old one to be picked last
The picker works from a printed pick note per customer, ticks off what has been picked and writes on it where a substitution was made
Lot numbers are again not captured at picking
Pick notes are kept in a drawer for a few months and then binned
bottlenecks_and_risks: Lot numbers are never captured at goods in or at picking, so a recall cannot be traced to specific customers at all
The only available response is to identify roughly when a delivery arrived and ring every customer who bought that product in the following two weeks - approximately 80 shops for a single product
No location system in the chiller defeats first in first out, so the oldest stock is picked last, increasing both waste and the age of any affected stock still on hand
Pick notes, the only picking record, are binned after a few months, so a recall on older stock has no record at all
The traceability process has never been tested, and a customer BRC-style audit is due in the autumn
Chilled lines including cooked meats, cheese and ready meals carry the highest food safety risk and the weakest records
recommended_improved_process: Capture lot number and best-before date at goods in, by scanning where the supplier provides a barcode
Introduce chiller locations and record put-away by location to enforce first in first out
Capture the lot picked against each customer order line at picking
Retain traceability records for at least the product shelf life plus the required retention period
Run a mock recall exercise and record the time taken and the accuracy of customer identification
Prepare the traceability evidence pack ahead of the autumn customer audit
ai_agent_steps: An AI agent can execute a recall trace, identifying affected customer orders from captured lot data within minutes
An AI agent can flag stock approaching best-before and highlight where first in first out has been breached by location
An AI agent can generate the customer notification list and draft recall notices for approval
An AI agent can compile the traceability evidence pack for the customer audit
human_approvals_controls: Steve or a nominated food safety lead authorises the issue of any recall notification to customers

INTERVIEWER: Safeguarding records. Talk me through it.
FARIDA: Every tutor has to have an enhanced DBS before they teach. That's non-negotiable, I'm strict on that.
INTERVIEWER: How do you know they have one?
FARIDA: They send me the certificate, usually a photo of it, and I put the number and the date on the spreadsheet.

FARIDA: It's a Google Sheet, "Tutor Records". Columns for name, DBS number, issue date, whether they're on the update service, safeguarding training date, and their references.

FARIDA: I stood him down for two weeks until it came through. He wasn't happy.
INTERVIEWER: Safeguarding training?
FARIDA: An online course, they send me the certificate PDF. I've got a Google Drive folder. Some are in there, some are only in my email.
INTERVIEWER: Are the certificates and the sheet reconciled?
FARIDA: No. The sheet says the date, the folder has the file, they don't always agree.
INTERVIEWER: References?
FARIDA: Two, by email. I chase them. About half never come back and I've let people start anyway.
INTERVIEWER: Does anything get reported externally?

TREATMENT ESTIMATES AND FINANCIAL CONSENT
Practice procedure note

Patients undergoing private treatment are to be given an estimate of the cost before treatment commences.

Current practice:

The clinician discusses the proposed treatment with the patient at the chair, usually at the examination appointment. The likely cost is stated verbally. Where the patient asks, alternatives at different price points are described.

Where the treatment is straightforward - a single filling, a hygiene appointment, a private crown - no written estimate is produced. The figure quoted is taken from the practice fee list, which the clinician recalls from memory. The fee list was last revised eighteen months ago and is displayed in the waiting room.

Where the treatment is complex - implants, multiple crowns, orthodontics - the practice manager is asked to prepare a written treatment plan. This is typed in Word from the clinician's handwritten note, printed, and either given to the patient at a subsequent visit or posted. Turnaround is described as "a few days to a fortnight".

Signed acceptance is obtained for complex plans only, and only where the patient attends to collect the plan.

Points noted at review: quoted figures given verbally are not recorded in the patient record, so where a patient later disputes the charge there is nothing to refer to. Different clinicians quote different figures for the same item. Laboratory charges have risen since the fee list was set and some crowns are being delivered below cost. No estimate is issued for treatment that changes mid-course, for example where a filling becomes a root canal. Patients are not told what is and is not included, particularly follow-up visits.

FUNCTION AND WEDDING CATERING - QUOTATION
Standing note, events file

The restaurant caters weddings and large private functions on site and, occasionally, at external venues.

Enquiry. Enquiries arrive via the website enquiry form, by telephone and by email. All are handled by the events coordinator, or by the owner where she is not available.

Quotation. A quotation is produced from a spreadsheet held on the office PC called "Function Pricing". The spreadsheet contains per-head food costs by menu, a margin multiplier, and lines for staffing, hire items, cake cutting, corkage and room dressing.

The food cost figures in the spreadsheet were entered when it was created and have not been revised. The events coordinator confirmed at review that she does not know when they were set, and that she was told to "add ten percent for the way things are now" by the owner as an interim measure.

The completed quotation is copied into an email and sent as text, not as an attachment. No PDF or letterhead document is produced.

Acceptance. The client replies by email. A deposit of £500 is requested to hold the date. There is no contract, no cancellation terms and no statement of what is included.

Variation. Guest numbers, menu choices and additions change repeatedly between booking and the event, often for a year or more. Changes are agreed by email and are not consolidated anywhere; the final invoice is built by reading back through the email chain.

Review. Actual food cost against quoted price is not calculated after an event. Gross margin on functions is not known. The kitchen has said several times that certain menus "lose money" but this has not been tested.

input:
Subject: how we price - or don't

Hi,

Been meaning to write this since we spoke.

We pitch for new business maybe twice a month. Brand work, campaigns, sometimes a retainer.

The pricing bit happens right at the end, usually the night before, and it's whoever's presenting who decides. They look at the scope, think about how many days it'll take, think about what the client can probably afford, and write a number.

There's no rate card that I know of. There might have been one. Different people use different day rates in their heads - I've heard £750 and I've heard £1,100 for the same seniority.

Nobody does a proper resource estimate. Nobody checks the number against what a similar job actually cost us, partly because I'm not sure we know what similar jobs cost us.

Sometimes a discount gets given in the room. That's not recorded anywhere.

We don't know our win rate. I'd guess a third? We don't log pitches.

We don't know if the ones we win are profitable. I think some of them definitely aren't - there's a rebrand from last year that everyone goes quiet about.

Who's responsible for pricing? Genuinely couldn't tell you. It's whoever's in front of the client.

I know this isn't a lot to go on. Happy to dig out whatever you need, though I'm not sure what exists.

[Instagram DM export, brand founder to a corporate buyer - shared during review]

BUYER: Hi! We're looking at your candles for a client gift, roughly 250 units, delivered before 12 Dec. Can you do a price?
KATIE (founder): Hi! Yes we can definitely do that. Let me have a think and come back to you 😊
[2 days later]
KATIE: Sorry for the delay! So for 250 we could do £16 each including a gift box, that's off our usual £24
BUYER: Great. Does that include the branded sleeve we discussed?
KATIE: Ah the sleeve - I'd need to check with the printer. Probably about £1.50 more?
BUYER: And delivery to two addresses?
KATIE: Should be fine!
BUYER: Can you put that in a formal quote for our procurement team? They need line items, VAT, lead time and payment terms.
KATIE: Of course, I'll get that over 😊

[Founder's note added for the review]
"This is normal for us. Corporate gifting is maybe 20% of Q4 but it all happens in DMs like this. I price it in my head. I don't have a cost per unit that includes the box, the sleeve, the tissue, or the extra labour for hand-tying 250 of them - I know the wax and vessel cost and I add to that. I've never done a formal quote document. When someone asks for one, like this, I panic and copy an invoice template. I don't put an expiry on it, and last year one came back and accepted a price four months later when my glass cost had gone up 30%. I also said yes to the two addresses without checking what a pallet split costs. I have no record of the quotes I've sent - they're in DMs across two accounts, my personal and the brand one. I couldn't tell you how many I sent last year or how many landed."

[Van cab, after a survey visit - owner and consultant]

CONSULTANT: You just quoted that job. Talk me through what happened.
GARETH: She wants the bathroom doing. I walked round, had a look at the pipework, checked where the soil stack is, asked what suite she wanted.
CONSULTANT: And you gave her a price?
GARETH: I said about four and a half, five grand depending on the tiles.
CONSULTANT: Verbally, at the door?
GARETH: Yeah. That's how it's always been. People want a number.
CONSULTANT: What happens next?
GARETH: I'll text her tonight. "Bathroom as discussed, £4,750, two weeks' work, can start w/c 14th."
CONSULTANT: That's the quote?
GARETH: That's the quote.
CONSULTANT: What's included?
GARETH: Well, she knows what we said.
CONSULTANT: Does she? Is the suite included?
GARETH: Supply and fit, yeah, up to a budget. I said a grand for the suite.
CONSULTANT: Is that in the text?
GARETH: It will be. Some of it.
CONSULTANT: Tiles?
GARETH: She's buying the tiles. I'll fit them.
CONSULTANT: What if she buys a mosaic that takes four days to lay?
GARETH: [pause] Yeah. That's happened.
CONSULTANT: Making good, plastering, waste removal, the electrics for the shower?
GARETH: Sparky's separate, she'll pay him direct. Plastering I'd sub out and I've allowed for it in my head.
CONSULTANT: Do you write down what you allowed?
GARETH: No.
CONSULTANT: How do you work out the price?
GARETH: Days times a day rate, plus materials, plus a bit.
CONSULTANT: What's the day rate?
GARETH: Depends how much I want the job.
CONSULTANT: Do you follow up if she doesn't reply?
GARETH: Not really. If they want it they ring.
CONSULTANT: How many of these do you do a week?
GARETH: Three or four.
CONSULTANT: How many turn into jobs?
GARETH: No idea. Half?

Discovery notes - accountancy practice, new business pricing (session ran short)

- Practice takes on maybe 40-60 new clients a year. Mix of sole traders, small limited companies, a few partnerships and landlords.

REFURBISHMENT QUOTATION HANDLING
Extract from office procedures folder, lettings & management department

Where a managed property requires works beyond routine repair, quotations are obtained from contractors and presented to the landlord for instruction.

Steps as currently performed:

(a) A need for works is identified, generally following a tenancy end and the check-out report, or following a tenant report of disrepair.
(b) Contractors known to the office are contacted and asked to attend and quote. The number of quotations obtained is not fixed.
(c) Contractors return quotations by email, in their own formats, at varying levels of detail. Some are a single line and a total; others are itemised.
(d) The quotations received are forwarded on to the landlord, generally as separate emails as they arrive.
(e) The landlord replies indicating which contractor to instruct, or asks questions, which are relayed back to the contractor.
(f) On instruction, the works are booked in.

Observations recorded at review: no covering summary or comparison is prepared for the landlord; no standard scope of works is issued to contractors, so quotations are not comparable; there is no target turnaround; and where a landlord does not reply the matter is not routinely chased. Quotations are not retained in any central location once forwarded.

Subject: the revision course pricing mess - can you help

Hi,

Following on from our chat at the school fair. So we run intensive revision courses at Easter and October half term - GCSE maths, English lit, the sciences, sometimes A-level chem if there's demand. Small groups, 5 days, usually in the church hall or the community centre.

The problem is nobody can tell me what one of these costs a parent. Genuinely. If a parent rings and I answer, I say £295 for the five days. If Jenny answers she says £275 because that's what it was two years ago and nobody told her. If Marcus answers - he's my most senior tutor and he does a lot of the enquiries in the evening - he'll quote per day, £65, so that's £325 if they do all five, and he'll also do a sibling discount off his own bat which I only find out about when the invoice doesn't match.

Then there's the ones where a parent wants three of the five days, or wants their child in the A-level group but they're in year 11, and everyone makes a different call on that.

The enquiry usually comes in by phone or the contact form on our site, or a parent grabs one of us at pickup. There's no form, no template. Whoever takes it just says a number and then emails the parent to confirm, or doesn't.

We use Google Workspace and a Google Sheet for the bookings, and Stripe payment links that I make manually. That's it really. No CRM.

I think we're leaving money on the table and also annoying people. What do you suggest?

Cheers
Ade

[Shop floor conversation, recorded with permission - independent bike shop, 2 branches]

CONSULTANT: Someone brings something back. What happens?
JAMIE (owner): Depends what and depends who's on.
CONSULTANT: Say it's a helmet, unworn, bought three weeks ago.
JAMIE: If I'm here I'd refund it. If it's still boxed and they've got the receipt, no argument.
CONSULTANT: And if there's no receipt?
JAMIE: I'd usually still do it if I recognise them or I can find the sale on the till. Our till is Lightspeed so I can search by card sometimes, if they paid by card and they know roughly when.
CONSULTANT: If they don't?
JAMIE: Credit note. Or I might just do it anyway if they're a regular. That's my call.
CONSULTANT: Who else can authorise a refund?
JAMIE: Anyone on the shop floor can do a refund on the till, there's no manager code. Ben in Chesterfield does what he thinks is right, and he's more generous than me.
CONSULTANT: Do you know how much you refund a month?
JAMIE: No. It'll be in Lightspeed somewhere as a negative sale but I've never looked.
CONSULTANT: What happens to the goods?
JAMIE: If it's sellable it goes back on the shelf. If it's a bike component that's been fitted and taken off, it goes in the box under the bench, and that box is... let's say it's full.
CONSULTANT: Anything written down?
JAMIE: No. Nothing.
CONSULTANT: Warranty returns to the supplier?
JAMIE: Different thing, that's an email to the rep and it takes weeks. Customers get annoyed because we can't tell them where it is.
CONSULTANT: Do you know your most-returned product?
JAMIE: Not a clue. Probably turbo trainers.

input:
Call notes - dental practice, implant and cosmetic work

Topic: refunds of treatment deposits where a patient cancels or does not proceed.

- Implant and larger cosmetic cases require a deposit at treatment planning stage. Deposits are typically 30-50% and can be £900-£3,500.
- Deposit is taken at reception by card, or by bank transfer for larger amounts, and recorded against the patient in SOE.
- Trigger for a refund request: patient cancels, changes their mind after a cooling-off conversation, or is found to be unsuitable at the CT stage.
- No written policy exists. The treatment plan letter says a deposit is "non-refundable" but the practice principal (Mr Achebe) has never enforced this.
- Decisions are made case by case by whoever the patient speaks to. Practice manager decides small ones; principal decides where he is asked. There is no threshold defining which is which.
- Costs already incurred - CT scan, lab-made surgical guide, planning time, blocked-out theatre sessions - are sometimes deducted and sometimes not. There is no schedule of what these cost.
- Refunds are processed on the card terminal and then entered into SOE separately. Reception said the two "sometimes drift".
- No record is kept of why a refund was given.
- Two refunds in the last year followed a threat to complain to the GDC. The practice manager considered these to have been "paid to make it go away".
- Nobody could say how many deposit refunds were made last year or their total value without going through the card machine reports line by line.

gold.trigger: A patient cancels, changes their mind after a cooling-off conversation, or is found to be unsuitable at the CT stage.

Call notes - restaurant group, 2 sites

Topic: deposits taken against bookings, and refunds where a booking is cancelled.

- Deposits are taken on larger bookings. The threshold varies - "eight or more, or ten, or if it's a Saturday in December". Not written down.
- Taken by card over the phone, or by a payment link, or occasionally bank transfer. Different managers use different methods.

- No log of refunds given, values, or reasons.
- Chargebacks: two in the last year. Both were lost because no evidence of the terms could be produced.
- Nobody could say what deposits are currently held or against which future bookings.

CREDIT NOTES AND CLIENT REBATES
Finance procedure note, media and performance team

Background. The agency buys paid media on behalf of clients. Where planned spend is not delivered in a period - a campaign starts late, a platform under-delivers, a budget is not fully spent - the client is due either a rebate of the management fee, a carry-forward of budget, or a credit note.

Current handling.

Identification. Under-delivery is identified by the performance team when they build the monthly client report, by comparing planned spend on the media plan against actual spend pulled from the platforms. This comparison is done manually in a spreadsheet per client.

Decision. The account director discusses the shortfall with the client, usually on the monthly call. The outcome - carry forward, credit note, or nothing - is negotiated in the conversation.

Authorisation. There is no approval threshold. Account directors agree credit notes of any value with the client directly. Finance is informed after the fact.

Processing. Finance raises the credit note in Xero against the original invoice on the account director's email instruction.

Recording. The reason for the credit note is entered as free text and varies widely. There is no code or category.

Issues recorded: total credit notes issued in the last financial year were £41,800 against fee income; this figure was not visible to the partners until year end. Three clients have carried budget forward for more than six months, creating a liability that is not tracked anywhere. Where a platform issues a make-good, it is not always passed to the client. Media plans exist as PDFs and are not versioned, so what was "planned" is contested.

input:
MEMBERSHIP CANCELLATION AND REFUNDS
Front desk procedure, independent health club

Members may cancel their membership by giving one calendar month's notice in writing, as set out in the membership terms. Requests for refunds arise where a member has paid in advance, where a direct debit has been taken after a cancellation was requested, or where a member cannot attend for a period.

Current handling:

1. The member contacts the club - by phone, at the desk, by email to the general address, or occasionally through the club's Facebook page.
2. Whoever receives the request deals with it. Front desk staff, the duty manager and the general manager all handle cancellations. There is no routing rule.
3. Where the member asks for money back, the person handling it decides. Front desk staff have processed refunds without reference to a manager.
4. Refunds are made either by reversing the direct debit collection, by bank transfer, or by refunding to a card at the desk. The method chosen varies.
5. The membership record in Legend is updated to cancelled, usually. Access cards are sometimes left active.
6. No note of the reason for cancellation is required, and the reason field is usually blank.

Points noted: the one month notice term is applied inconsistently - some staff waive it on request, others enforce it. Members who complain more assertively receive more. There is no record of refunds granted by value or by staff member. Cancellations are not counted or reported to the owner other than as a net membership figure. No attempt is made to save the membership - there is no retention conversation, offer of a freeze, or exit question. Members who cancel their direct debit at the bank without notifying the club are identified only when the payment fails.

input:
Subject: returns - it's worse than I told you on the call

Hi Rachel,

I need to correct something I said. I told you our returns process is "Leah scans it back in". That's what I thought happened. I sat with her yesterday and it isn't.

What actually happens: parcel comes back to the unit. There's a bin by the door. Everything goes in the bin - returns, samples, wholesale rejects, stuff the carrier failed to deliver, all of it.

Leah works through the bin when she can. She opens the parcel, finds the printed packing slip if the customer put it back in, and looks up the order in Shopify by the order number on the slip. Then she checks the item's sellable, and refunds in Shopify.

If there's no slip - and I'd say that's a third of them - she tries to work out who it is from the return address on the label. If she can't, it goes in the "mystery" pile. That pile is currently about forty parcels going back to the summer.

Here's my problem. I asked her how long it takes from a parcel arriving to a refund and she said two to three days. Our customer service inbox has emails from people who returned things four and five weeks ago asking where their money is, and Leah showed me the Shopify refunds and there are ones dated six weeks after the tracking said delivered to us. So both of those can't be right. I don't think she's lying, I think she genuinely believes she's on top of it because the front of the bin is recent and the back of it isn't.

We don't have a returns portal. We tell people to email for an address. We don't ask a reason, so I've got no idea why anything comes back. We don't check whether the item was faulty or just not wanted, and we don't charge for return postage or not charge, consistently - Leah decides.

Ben

[Partners' meeting, extract - accountancy practice]

KEVIN: Item four, the write-offs. Angela, you wanted this on.
ANGELA: I did. I pulled the numbers. We wrote off £68,000 of billed fees last year.
KEVIN: That can't be right.
ANGELA: It's the credit notes and the manual adjustments in Xero together. I've got the list.
KEVIN: How is anyone writing off that much?
ANGELA: We are. All of us. A client rings and says the bill's too high, and whoever they get says "leave it with me, I'll sort it", and then raises a credit.
KEVIN: I'd only do that for a good reason.
ANGELA: I'm sure. But there's no record of the reason. The credit note narration says "as agreed" on about half of them.
DAVID: Is there a limit?
ANGELA: No. Any of the four of us can raise one for any amount. And so can Priya in the office if one of us asks her to.
DAVID: Do we ever look at them?
ANGELA: We're doing it now, for the first time.
KEVIN: What's driving them?
ANGELA: I can tell you what I think, not what the data says, because there isn't any. I think it's mostly jobs that overran and we didn't tell the client until the invoice landed. And some of it is the fixed fee not covering what we actually did, so the client's surprised.
DAVID: Are the same clients doing this repeatedly?
ANGELA: I'd have to go through it by hand. There's no client-level view.
KEVIN: What about the partner-level view?
ANGELA: [pause] I did look. It's not even.
KEVIN: Right.
ANGELA: I'd also say - none of this goes back to the person who did the work. The team don't know their job was written down. So nothing changes.

input:
[Reception, salon - manager and consultant]

CONSULTANT: Someone brings back a shampoo. What happens?
DENISE: We take it back.
CONSULTANT: Always?
DENISE: Pretty much. It's not worth the argument over a £22 bottle. We give them the money or swap it for something else.
CONSULTANT: Receipt?
DENISE: We ask. Half of them haven't got one. If they bought it here we'd probably know - we know our clients.
CONSULTANT: How would you check?
DENISE: You could look in Fresha if it went through as a retail item on their account. But a lot of retail goes through as a walk-in sale with no client attached, so then you can't.
CONSULTANT: What are the usual reasons?
DENISE: "It didn't suit my hair." "It made it greasy." Sometimes a stylist has recommended something wrong for them, which is on us.
CONSULTANT: What do you do with the returned bottle?
DENISE: If it's sealed it goes back on the shelf. If it's been opened it goes in the staff room and the girls use it.
CONSULTANT: Is the stock adjusted?
DENISE: [pause] No. I don't think anyone does that.
CONSULTANT: So the shelf quantity in Fresha stays as if it sold?
DENISE: It'd be sold and then refunded, so it should go back. But only if you do it as a proper refund on the item. Sometimes the girls just give cash out of the till.
CONSULTANT: Out of the till, no transaction?
DENISE: It happens.
CONSULTANT: Is there a batch or expiry check?
DENISE: No.
CONSULTANT: A time limit?
DENISE: No.
CONSULTANT: Does anyone track how much comes back?
DENISE: No. But I know the retail figures never quite make sense.
CONSULTANT: Does the stylist who recommended it hear about it?
DENISE: No, and they should, because their commission's on the sale.
CONSULTANT: Is the commission clawed back?
DENISE: No.

input:
Notes - lettings, end of tenancy deposit deductions (partial session)

- Deposits are protected in a government-approved scheme. Where a landlord wishes to make a deduction and the tenant disagrees, the scheme adjudicates on the evidence submitted.
- The firm's record over the last two years was described as "we lose most of them". No figures were available.
- Process on paper: check-out report compared to the check-in inventory; deductions proposed; tenant agrees or disputes; if disputed, evidence goes to the scheme.
- Where the evidence sits was not established. The inventory pads are filed somewhere in the office. Check-in photographs are on a phone or several phones. Check-out photographs are taken by whoever does the check-out. Some are emailed in, some are not.
- Nobody could say whether photographs are dated or whether the date is retained when they are emailed.
- Cleaning and repair quotes used to justify a deduction: sometimes obtained, sometimes estimated by the negotiator.
- Correspondence with the tenant about the deduction is by email from individual staff accounts, so it is not all in one place.
- Deadlines: the scheme sets time limits for responding. Two claims in the last year were lost because the response was late. Who is responsible for watching the deadline could not be established.
- No template is used for the deduction proposal. Wording varies.
- Fair wear and tear is applied inconsistently; there is no depreciation guide in use.
- Landlords are told the outcome by email. Where a deduction fails, the landlord sometimes asks the firm to cover it. It was not clear what happens then.
- No log of disputes, outcomes, or reasons is kept.

input:
Call notes - distributor, customer returns of unsold stock

- Trade customers - mainly convenience stores - return stock that has not sold. Slow lines, seasonal items after the season, and occasionally a whole planogram change.
- No returns policy exists. Sales reps agree returns with customers on the spot to keep them sweet.
- Trigger: the customer tells the rep or rings the sales desk. The rep tells the driver to collect it on the next delivery.
- The driver picks up whatever is put in front of him. He writes "collection" on the POD, sometimes with a case count, sometimes not.
- The stock comes back to the warehouse and is left in a bay by the goods-in door.
- A credit is raised by the sales office on the customer's word about what was sent back, before anyone has looked at it.
- Nobody checks condition, date code, or whether it is even our stock. Two pallets of a competitor's product were credited last year.
- Date-expired and damaged goods in the returns bay are eventually skipped. No write-off is posted against the credit.
- The bay currently holds stock estimated by the warehouse manager at "eight, ten pallets", some of it more than a year old.
- No analysis of which customers or lines drive returns.
